    Our feedforward model is trained on a randomly sampled subset of Objaverse with 32k assets. We evaluate on 30 unseen Objaverse assets and 30 ShapeNet assets to compare with per-object methods. The same metrics dₚₘ, dₙₒᵣₘ as in Section4.1 are used, along with PSNR for appearance reconstruction.

    Evaluation.

    We evaluate a shared feedforward checkpoint under the same rendering and scoring protocol used for the per-object methods. Ours-F retains the direct ray-query interface without per-object fitting. On Objaverse, its reconstruction is comparable to VQAD: it has substantially lower positional error, while VQAD remains stronger on normal accuracy and PSNR. On ShapeNet, Ours-F improves all three reported metrics over VQAD, showing that the same structured output space remains effective after the dataset shift.

    Efficiency.

    Table3 reports practical fitting times of each method. N-BVH requires about 3 minutes and VQAD requires tens of minutes of optimization for each object. In contrast, our feedforward model constructs a renderable representation from a colored point cloud in 50 ms with 19.5 hours for training paid once across all objects. As shown in Table3, this removes per-object optimization while retaining competitive reconstruction quality.

    Generalization.

    The shared model is trained on Objaverse and evaluated on ShapeNet without retraining. Despite this distribution shift, our feedforward model outperforms both VQAD and N-BVH on ShapeNet, although both baselines optimize each object separately. This result shows that the octree feature extractor and intersection decoder transfer across datasets while preserving the directly renderable output space.

    4.3 Applications

    Photorealistic Rendering with Ray Tracing.

    Since the decoder returns a hit, position, normal, and albedo, NeuOctree can be queried directly by a surface ray tracer. It supports reshading, reflection, refraction, and a fisheye projection without mesh extraction or texture baking (Fig.7).

    Native 3D Generation.

    NeuOctree can also serve as the native output of an image-conditioned generator. A sparse-octree VAE compresses node features, and a flow-matching DiT predicts occupancy and latent features that decode directly into renderable geometry and appearance. Each example in Fig.8 shows the conditioning image, surface normal, and albedo.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented NeuOctree, a neural explicit surface representation for ray tracing. Shared corner features in a sparse octree and a recurrent decoder jointly predict ray–surface hits, positions, normals, and albedo, supporting compact geometry–appearance modeling, direct rendering, and open surfaces. Experiments show accurate reconstruction across meshes and budgets; the shared feedforward model constructs a renderable representation in about 50 ms, rather than minutes of per-object optimization, and transfers from Objaverse to ShapeNet without retraining. Ray-traced rendering and image-conditioned generation further demonstrate the versatility of this structured output space.

    NeuOctree still requires costly high-fidelity per-object fitting and models albedo rather than view-dependent materials; generation remains a proof of concept. Future work will accelerate octree construction, extend surface queries to richer materials, lighting, and dynamics, and develop NeuOctree as a native output space for 3D generative models.

    AI use statement

    In this work, we used a generative AI coding assistant to assist with limited code debugging, migrate the existing manuscript into the ICLR 2027 LaTeX template, proofread the language, and check compilation and formatting. It was not used to produce the research ideas, experimental results, figures, or scientific claims in this paper. The authors reviewed the revised source and take responsibility for the final content of this work.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Experimental Details and Additional Results

    This appendix records the configurations that determine the entries in the main paper, with particular emphasis on the capacity-matched comparison in Table1. We separate the per-object optimization setting from the shared feedforward model because their stored state and training protocols are fundamentally different.

    A.1 Common Evaluation Protocol

    Objects and cameras.

    The geometry-compression benchmark contains Armadillo, Buddha, Dragon, Einstein, Lucy, Metatron, and XYZ-Dragon. Every method is scored from the same 16 fixed cameras at 512×512 resolution, with a 60^∘ field of view and a camera distance of 2.5 after normalizing the longest bounding-box edge to 2. We use the same per-object coordinate convention and camera conversion for all methods.

    Metrics.

    The evaluation mask is the union of the ground-truth and predicted foreground masks. The position metric dₚₘ is the mean Euclidean distance between corresponding ray intersections in normalized object coordinates and is reported after multiplication by 10³. The normal metric dₙₒᵣₘ is the mean oriented angular error in degrees. Appearance experiments additionally report RGB PSNR. Some evaluation implementations store dₚₘ after multiplication by 10⁴; those values are divided by ten before insertion into the paper.

    Payload accounting.

    The four nominal targets are 82,944, 124,928, 249,856, and 842,752 bytes, reported as 81, 122, 244, and 823 KiB. A payload includes all object-specific state required by a method at inference time. Shared weights of the feedforward model are excluded from its per-object representation size. The tables below record the actual configuration and measured payload used for each of the 28 cells of every method. We use the abbreviations D (octree depth), F (feature dimension or requested/coarse faces, as specified by the caption), H (decoder width), L (octree level), B (codebook bit width), Q (coarse quads), N (BVH nodes), and P (measured payload in bytes).

    A.2 Feedforward NeuOctree

    Input representation and architecture.

    The reported feedforward model is the depth-9 union variant. For each object, its input octree is the union of a conservatively rasterized depth-9 mesh occupancy (with colors sampled from eight rendered albedo views) and a 200k point cloud. The union is capped at 900,000 depth-9 cells; this cap limits the encoder memory without changing the depth-7 coverage used by the renderer. The octree uses full_depth=4 and query depth 7. Its nine LPF input channels encode position, within-cell offset, and local color. A sparse octree U-Net maps the depth-9 input to 128 channels at query depth 7. These channels are reshaped into eight 16-dimensional corner features per voxel and averaged at shared corners, yielding the continuous vertex feature field used by the renderer. The renderer has hidden width 128, four recurrent refinements, 8-dimensional voxel features, RMSNorm, and segment-position encoding. Its hit threshold is 0.4, and the forward pass is chunked at 65,536 candidates (with a maximum render batch of 262,144 queries).

    Figure 9 details the 3D U-Net used by the feedforward encoder. The sparse octree input and point-cloud features enter a multiscale encoder, are fused at the bottleneck, and are decoded with skip connections to produce the output octree and point features. Each octree residual block uses two 1×1 convolutions with RMSNorm and ReLU, followed by a residual addition and a final ReLU, as shown in the lower panel.

    Losses.

    The hit term uses balanced binary cross-entropy with positive weight 1.5, Tversky weight 0.2 and (α,β,γ)=(0.3,0.7,1.0). Hole, floater, and boundary penalties have weights 0.1, 0.1, and 0.2. Color uses weight 2.0, a Charbonnier penalty, gradient weight 0.2, and masked SSIM weight 0.5. Normal supervision uses cosine weight 0.1, gradient weight 0.3, and masked SSIM weight 0.3. We additionally use parameter ℓ₂ regularization of 10⁻³, ray-distance weight 0.5, final-stage weight 0.5, and detail scale 4.0.

    Training and inference time.

    The reported d9-union model was selected on the full 1,000-object validation set with a selection score of 1.3781. It was trained from random initialization for three epochs (180,000 optimizer steps) on four RTX 3090 GPUs, corresponding to approximately 50.6 h of uninterrupted training. Building the depth-9 occupancy cache is a separate one-time cost of approximately 5.2 h and 91 GB. The 19.5 h figure in the main paper is the eight-GPU equivalent estimated from measured per-iteration throughput. These training costs are not comparable to the per-object timing table. Inference timing excludes data loading, rendering, and metric evaluation.

    Stored representation size.

    The shared feedforward network has 36.888M parameters and is not replicated per object. Per-object state consists of depth-7 topology, a 16-dimensional fp16 vertex field, and an optional 8-dimensional fp16 voxel field. The 128-channel U-Net output is an intermediate tensor and is not stored. With the voxel field enabled, the seven reference objects occupy 381–1,674 KiB (806 KiB on average); without it, they occupy 304–1,372 KiB (654 KiB on average).

    A.3 Complete Capacity Configurations for Table 1

    NeuOctree (per-object optimization).

    For every cell, we optimize a geometry-only NeuOctree for 300 epochs over 242 training views, using two RTX 4090 GPUs with pair-balanced DDP. The optimizer uses an initial learning rate of 2×10⁻³ with linear decay to 10⁻⁵. We use three decoder refinements, recurrent-pool sampling, no voxel-feature branch, and fp16 storage. Each entry below is D/F/H followed by the measured payload. The feature dimension and decoder width are jointly selected to fill the target budget; consequently, they vary across both objects and rates. Table5 reports the complete settings.

    NGF.

    We keep the upstream NGF network fixed (20 features, eight Fourier-feature levels, batch size 10, and a fixed seed); only the coarse quad mesh changes the object-specific payload. Training uses four resolution levels, 100 iterations per level, batch size 10, and 200 reference views on one RTX 4090. Each entry in Table7 is requested faces F, realized coarse quads Q, and measured payload P. The paper metrics are recomputed with the common 16-view union-mask evaluator, not NGF’s native held-out-view evaluator.

    QNDF.

    QNDF is run for 4,000 optimizer iterations on one RTX 4090. Its size is controlled by the realized coarse-mesh face count F and decoder width H. Entries in Table7 are F/H and measured payload. The Dragon 823 KiB cell is an exception: a request for 1,900 faces produced a remeshed surface with 12,798 faces and 6,381 vertices, explaining its larger run time relative to the other cells at this rate.

    VQAD.

    We adapt VQAD to six-channel geometry supervision (normal and normalized position), use four LODs, and optimize for 100 epochs over 242 training views with RMSprop at 10⁻³ and AMP. Table 1 uses the actual evaluated configuration for each cell: two 81 KiB cells use the final 3-bit setting, 13 further cells use uniform splitting, and the remaining cells use the settings listed in Table9. Entries are L/B/F/H/K, where K is the number of decoder layers, followed by payload P.

    N-BVH.

    N-BVH uses four features per level, eight levels, 64 neurons, four hidden layers, WorldT depth learning, a last split at iteration 3,000, split and split-interval scale factors of 2, and 10,000 training steps on one RTX 4090. The hash-map sizes are 2⁹, 2⁹, 2¹⁰, and 2¹¹ across the four rates. Capacity is controlled by split intervals 235, 100, 60, and 28, producing the node counts in Table9. Entries are node count N and payload P.

    A.4 Training Hardware and Runtime

    All per-object timing runs were executed on the same RTX 4090 server. Ours uses two GPUs with DDP; each baseline uses one GPU. The values in Table10 are wall-clock minutes per object, averaged over all seven meshes. They are practical end-to-end fitting costs under each method’s own training budget, rather than equal-GPU or equal-step throughput measurements. The N-BVH times exclude the separate capacity-calibration probe. The VQAD timing sweep uses a uniform 65,536-sample protocol for all 28 cells; its timing configurations may therefore differ from the quality configurations in Table9.

    Feedforward training uses four RTX 3090 GPUs. The capacity and timing experiments use the GPU allocations reported in Table10, and the generation experiments use four RTX 5090 GPUs. We report only the devices allocated to each experiment rather than the total capacity of the host.

    A.5 Native 3D Generation Details

    The generation demonstration uses NeuOctree itself as the output domain. A sparse-octree VAE encodes the occupancy and feature tensors of a renderable NeuOctree into an 8³ latent grid. An image-conditioned flow-matching DiT predicts both latent features and occupancy; the VAE decoder then reconstructs the octree feature field, which can be queried by the same surface renderer as the reconstructed assets. No mesh extraction or post-hoc texture baking is required, and the paper does not use this experiment for a quantitative comparison with external generation systems.

    The generation setup uses 5,000 ShapeNet objects from ten categories. The VAE receives a 128³ representation, downsamples it four times to 8³, and uses a latent dimension of 32. It is trained with AdamW (learning rate 10⁻⁴, weight decay 0.01), batch size 32, on four RTX 5090 GPUs. For the image-conditioned model, 16 random Blender views are rendered per asset, with one retained for testing. The DiT has approximately 0.7B parameters: width 1,536, 16 transformer blocks, 12 attention heads, and MLP width 8,192. It uses the same optimizer settings, batch size 16, and four RTX 5090 GPUs.

    A.6 Reproducibility Notes and Limitations

    The capacity tables report measured payloads rather than inferring size from a compression-ratio label. The actual capacity controls are the values in Tables5, 7, 7, 9 and 9. The VQAD quality table uses the tested configuration listed for each cell, whereas its timing table uses a uniform 28-cell protocol. QNDF’s Dragon 823 KiB remeshing exception and N-BVH’s excluded calibration probe are disclosed above. Finally, the feedforward inference time measures representation construction only; image rendering and evaluation are separate downstream operations.

    A.7 Additional Qualitative Results

    Figure11 supplies the four Table 1 objects not shown in the main qualitative compression figure. The N-BVH render uses its method background, which is retained rather than cosmetically altered.

    Figure11 shows seven further Objaverse objects under a matched view. NeuOctree-F preserves large color regions and thin structures without per-object fitting; VQAD is often similarly sharp, whereas N-BVH more frequently exhibits color fragmentation or smoothing at the same nominal 823 KiB budget.

item.title: 一段视频长出声音和 360 度背景：SonoWorld4D 把单目视频变成可探索的 4D 视听场景 ｜ SonoWorld4D: From One Video to a 4D Audio-Visual Scene via Diffusion Synchronization
item.description:
一句话：4D 场景生成一直缺声音这一维；这条定义 Video-to-4DAVScene 任务并给出一套同步框架。

要点：

  • 新任务 Video-to-4DAVScene：把一段视频变成可探索、随时间变化的 4D 视听场景——声音本来与动态物体和事件强耦合，但此前工作基本没有建模
  • 给定单目视频，方法生成 360° 静态背景、重建前景动态内容，再把声音与动态事件同步起来
  • 关键手段是扩散同步（diffusion synchronization）：让画面与声音在时间上对齐，而不是各自生成后硬拼

为什么值得看：游戏与 XR 的环境音一直是手工铺的。如果「一段视频 → 可走进去 + 自带对应声音」成立，那么实景转场景的资产管线会多出一条声音通道，而且声音是跟着事件走的。

中文摘要：视觉场景生成已从静态 3D 走向「从极少输入生成动态 4D 场景」，但声音——本应与动态物体和事件强耦合——在此前的工作里几乎未被建模。这篇定义了 Video-to-4DAVScene 任务：把一段视频变成可探索、随时间变化的 4D 视听场景，并给出 SonoWorld4D 框架。给定单目视频，方法生成 360 度静态背景、重建前景动态内容，并通过扩散同步让声音与画面事件在时间上对齐，而不是各自生成后拼接。它的价值在于把「声音」纳入 4D 场景的表示里，从而让「实景转可走进去的场景」这条管线多出一条与事件同步的音频通道。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-29

本期推送：2026-11-02

SonoWorld4D: From One Video to a 4D Audio-Visual Scene via Diffusion Synchronization

Abstract

Recent progress in visual scene generation has extended beyond static 3D scenes toward the more challenging problem of generating dynamic 4D scenes from minimal input. However, sound, despite being intrinsically coupled with dynamic objects and events, remains largely unmodeled in prior work. We introduce Video-to-4DAVScene, a new task that turns a video into an explorable, time-varying 4D audio-visual scene, and present the SonoWorld4D framework for this task. Given a monocular video, our method generates a 360∘ static background, reconstructs explicit motion trajectories of dynamic, sound-emitting foreground objects, and synthesizes a dynamic sound field consistent across multiple sources through dual-space diffusion synchronization. The resulting 4D scene supports real-time novel-view visual and spatial audio rendering. Experiments on real-world dynamic scenes and a user study demonstrate that SonoWorld4D generates 4D audio-visual scenes with perceptually realistic, physically grounded spatial audio consistent with scene geometry and visual content.

https://humathe.github.io/sonoworld4d

1 Introduction

Advances in 3D scene reconstruction and generation [(Mildenhall et al., 2020; Kerbl et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2025a; Yu et al., 2024)], and more recently in dynamic 4D scene generation [(Wu et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2025; Lei et al., 2024)], make it possible to transform monocular videos into explorable, time-varying worlds with moving objects and temporally coherent geometry. Yet these worlds remain incomplete without sound, which is intrinsically coupled with dynamic objects and events: engine and wheel noise grow louder as a car approaches, sweeping past and fading into the distance; a dancer’s tap shoes strike the stage in sharp, rhythmic beats synchronized with each step; and ambient sounds such as wind and crowds continuously convey the structure and scale of the environment.

Despite its importance, limited prior work has modeled spatial audio in 3D visual scenes. Existing approaches either focus on static scenes without time-varying geometry or moving sound sources [(Jin et al., 2026; Yoshida et al., 2026)], or spatialize audio for dynamic videos under constrained camera and interaction settings [(Xie et al., 2025)]. Generating fully explorable 4D audio-visual scenes therefore remains an open challenge, requiring joint modeling of dynamic geometry, moving sound sources, and spatial audio.

We introduce Video-to-4DAVScene, a new problem that aims to turn a monocular video into an explorable 4D audio-visual scene: an interactive, time-varying world-space scene with dynamic sound sources that supports synchronized rendering of both visual content and spatial audio from novel viewpoints and listener trajectories. The generated scene should contain a spatially grounded sound field: ambient sound should be tied to the static environment, dynamic sounds should follow moving visual objects, and the rendered audio should remain consistent as the virtual listener moves through the reconstructed 4D audio-visual world.

Solving this problem introduces several new challenges. First, unlike recent 4D visual generation methods that primarily optimize visual fidelity, 4D audio-visual scene generation requires explicit scene geometry, camera motion, dynamic object trajectories, and static-dynamic structure to place and render sound sources in a physically meaningful coordinate system. Second, dynamic scenes contain heterogeneous acoustic components: ambient sound should align with the background, localized static sources should remain fixed in world space, and dynamic sources should follow foreground objects while obeying distance attenuation, occlusion, and motion-dependent effects. Third, the system must maintain consistency across coordinate spaces: input audio is observed in camera space, object sounds are represented in object-centric canonical space, and the output must be rendered for arbitrary listener trajectories in world space. These spaces must be synchronized to keep sound temporally aligned with the input video and geometrically consistent with the evolving scene.

To address these challenges, we propose SonoWorld4D, a world-space framework for 4D audio-visual scene generation. Given an input video, we reconstruct a decomposed 4D visual scene representation, comprising a 360^∘ static background and dynamic foreground objects with world-space trajectories, providing geometry and motion for spatial audio rendering while supporting interactive visual exploration. Building on this representation, we introduce a diffusion-based synchronization mechanism that jointly synthesizes a global camera-space audio signal and per-object canonical audio signals to generate a dynamic spatial sound field. Specifically, it repeatedly projects object-space sounds into camera space through acoustic rendering and maps the global mixture back to object space via inverse rendering, enforcing cross-space consistency throughout the diffusion process. This synchronization keeps the generated audio aligned with the input video while preserving persistent, re-renderable object sounds that follow dynamic sources under novel listener trajectories.

We evaluate SonoWorld4D on real-world dynamic scenes with moving foreground sound sources exhibiting rigid-body, human, and general deformable motion. We also establish objective evaluation protocols for Video-to-4DAVScene to assess the spatial accuracy and semantic consistency of generated audio. Experiments show that our framework generates 4D audio-visual scenes with spatial audio that better aligns with scene geometry, object motion, and listener viewpoint than baseline methods. Ablation studies and a user study further confirm the effectiveness of diffusion synchronization in generating coherent spatial audio with multiple sound sources.

2 Related Work

4D Visual Scene Generation. Recent 4D scene generation methods can be broadly grouped into video diffusion, dynamic Gaussian reconstruction, and dynamic foreground reconstruction. Video diffusion based methods  [(Ren et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2025b; Lin et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Bai et al., 2025)] synthesize photorealistic videos under controlled camera trajectories, but are trajectory-specific and often lack explicit geometry grounding. Dynamic Gaussian reconstruction methods  [(Lei et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Shih et al., 2025)] reconstruct geometry-grounded dynamic scenes from monocular videos and support real-time rendering, but are largely limited to visible regions and cannot reliably recover unseen object surfaces or a complete panoramic background. Dynamic foreground reconstruction methods further recover animatable 4D assets from monocular inputs, including category-agnostic deformable or articulated objects [(Liao et al., 2025; Sabathier et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Chen et al., 2025a; Litman et al., 2026)] and human-specific avatars [(Qiu et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024; Moon et al., 2024)]. Our visual pipeline builds on these advances to construct a 4D visual scene representation, combining dynamic foreground objects with a static background to enable generation of a dynamic spatial sound field.

Spatial Audio Generation. Audio generation methods synthesize realistic monaural audio from text or video [(Cheng et al., 2025; Shan et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b)], but typically lack spatial cues. Complementary approaches spatialize existing audio: RIR-based rendering and acoustic-field methods model propagation effects  [(Chen et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2024; Jin and Gao, 2025; Lan et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025b)], while visually guided methods use scene geometry, object locations, or motion to predict binaural or spatial audio from mono input [(Gao and Grauman, 2019; Garg et al., 2023; Garg et al., 2021; Morgado et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018; Liang et al., 2023)]. More recent methods generate ambisonics from videos [(Kim et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a; Lan et al., 2026)], spatialize generated audio for 4D scene exploration [(Xie et al., 2025)], or construct static 3D audio-visual scenes from single images [(Jin et al., 2026; Yoshida et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a)]. In contrast, SonoWorld4D generates explorable dynamic 4D audio-visual scenes with moving sound sources, synchronizing spatial audio with object motion while modeling listener-dependent acoustic effects.

Diffusion Synchronization. Diffusion synchronization couples multiple diffusion trajectories at inference time to satisfy shared constraints. Primarily explored for image generation, it enables coherent large images and region-controlled layouts [(Bar-Tal et al., 2023)], enforces consistency across overlapping generations [(Lee et al., 2023)], and models correlations between coupled trajectories [(Lee et al., 2025)]. Recent work extends these ideas to synchronize image and audio diffusion on a shared canvas [(Chen et al., 2024)] and extend long-form audio separation beyond the training length [(Shi et al., 2025)]. We also apply diffusion synchronization to audio, but target spatial audio rendering. Specifically, we synchronize camera-space and object-space audio trajectories through forward and inverse acoustic rendering, allowing generated source sounds to remain consistent with the camera-space mixture while being re-renderable under source motion and novel listener trajectories. To our knowledge, this is the first use of diffusion synchronization for spatial audio generation with an explicit rendering component.

3 The Video-to-4DAVScene Task

We define Video-to-4DAVScene as the problem of generating an explorable 4D audio-visual scene from a single monocular video. Given an input video V={Iₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ, where Iₜ denotes the RGB frame at time t, the problem is to generate:

V↦{S,A},

(1)

where S denotes a time-varying 4D visual scene with moving objects and A denotes a dynamic spatial sound field associated with the scene. The output should be explorable: for any target camera/listener trajectory, it should support synchronized novel-view visual rendering and listener-dependent spatial audio rendering.

Formally, given a target trajectory pₜ=[Rₜ,xₜ]∈SE(3), where Rₜ and xₜ denote the listener orientation and position at time t, the generated scene should render an audio-visual sequence

{S(pₜ),A(pₜ)}={Îᵖₜ, âᵖₜ}.

(2)

Here, Îᵖₜ is the visual observation rendered from pose pₜ, and âᵖₜ is the synchronized spatial audio perceived by the listener at the same pose. The visual scene S contains both the static environment and time-varying foreground content. The spatial sound field A should be geometrically and temporally grounded in S: ambient sound and static localized sound sources should remain fixed in static world space, and dynamic sound sources should move consistently with their corresponding foreground objects. Thus, the generated audio should not only match the semantic and temporal content of the input video, but also vary coherently with listener position, listener orientation, source motion, distance attenuation, and visibility.

The SonoScene4D Dataset. To support quantitative evaluation of this new task, we collect SonoScene4D, an evaluation dataset of 54 clips of dynamic scenarios with moving sound sources such as cars and humans. Specifically, each scene contains an 8-second 360∘ video captured at 30 FPS using an Insta360 X5 camera, paired with synchronized first-order ambisonic (FOA) audio recorded at 48 kHz using a RØDE NT-SF1 microphone placed at a novel listening pose. The FOA microphone is placed at a listening pose different from the camera pose, enabling evaluation of whether a method can render spatial audio at a novel listener location rather than merely reproducing camera-view audio. Further details about SonoScene4D are provided in Appendix (Sec. E).

Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate spatial audio generation in terms of spatial accuracy and semantic consistency. For spatial accuracy, we report correlation coefficient (CC) and area under the curve (AUC) between generated and reference spatial energy maps [(Kim et al., 2025)], together with direction-of-arrival (DoA) errors, including absolute azimuth error Δ_absθ, absolute elevation error Δ_absφ, and angular error Δ_Angular[(Liu et al., 2025a)]. For semantic consistency, we compute CLAP similarity between the rendered audio and manually annotated object descriptions. Spatial metrics are evaluated at 5 Hz and averaged over time, while CLAP is computed at the clip level.

4 Approach

4.1 Overview

Given a monocular video V={Iₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ, SonoWorld4D generates an explorable 4D audio-visual scene {S,A}. We distinguish three coordinate systems: world space is the shared, fixed reference frame for the scene; camera space is the camera’s coordinate system at each frame; and object space is the local coordinate system attached to each foreground object. To support object-space audio modeling, we decompose dynamic foreground objects from the static background and explicitly model each object’s trajectory, allowing its sound to follow its motion even when multiple objects move independently. All static objects are treated as part of the background. We represent the visual scene as S=(G_bgʷᵒʳˡᵈ,{Gᵢʷᵒʳˡᵈ}ᵢ₌₁^N), where G_bgʷᵒʳˡᵈ denotes the static background and Gᵢʷᵒʳˡᵈ denotes the i-th dynamic foreground object, both represented by Gaussians that support real-time rendering.

We represent the spatial sound field as:

A=(aᵃᵐᵇ,{aⱼᵇᵍ}ⱼ₌₁^M,{aᵢᵒᵇʲ}ᵢ₌₁^N),

(3)

where aᵃᵐᵇ denotes diffuse ambient audio, aⱼᵇᵍ denotes audio from the j-th static background source, and aᵢᵒᵇʲ denotes object-space audio from the i-th dynamic source. The reconstructed audio-visual scene provides the source locations, trajectories, and geometry required to render these signals from arbitrary listener poses.

Fig. 2 illustrates our framework. We first reconstruct a decomposed 4D visual scene in world space (Sec. 4.2): the static component provides geometry and context for ambient sound, while the dynamic component provides object-centric trajectories for moving sound sources. We then reconstruct a dynamic spatial sound field (Sec. 4.3) by jointly generating object-space and camera-space audio through diffusion synchronization, allowing source sounds to remain aligned with object motion and consistent with the rendered camera mixture. During free-viewpoint rendering (Sec. 4.4), a target listener trajectory is used to render novel-view visuals and spatialize the generated object sounds into synchronized audio coherently blended with the background sound.

4.2 4D Visual Scene Generation via Foreground-Background Decomposition

We first preprocess the input video to estimate scene geometry, camera poses, and foreground masks. Conditioned on the observed background regions and visible foreground pixels, we then generate panoramic background Gaussians and dynamic foreground Gaussians, respectively. Foreground generation supports three motion types: rigid-body, human, and general deformable motion, using a shared formulation for object motion estimation and deformable Gaussian generation. Finally, we align the generated foreground objects and background in a common world frame. The resulting 4D scene provides the geometry and object trajectories used for spatial audio generation and rendering.

Video Preprocessing. Given an input video {Iₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ with T frames, we use a geometry foundation model [(Wang et al., 2026)] to estimate depth maps {Dₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ and camera poses {Tₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ, and use a segmentation model [(Carion et al., 2026)] to obtain foreground masks {M_i,t}_i=1,t=1^N\hskip8.19447pt T, where N is the number of foreground objects. We further use a vision-language model (VLM) [(Team et al., 2026)] to infer acoustic context from the video. It produces a video-level description d_vid capturing the overall acoustic scene, including ambient and background sounds, and an object-level description dᵢ for each sound-producing foreground object i, capturing its sound semantics and temporal activity. The former conditions camera-space audio generation, while the latter conditions the corresponding object-space source generation in Sec. 4.3.

Panoramic Background Generation. We generate the background from observed background regions in the input video. To consolidate these observations into a single panorama for completion, we select the frame with the largest visible background region as an anchor frame and take its coordinate system as the world frame. We then unproject background pixels from the depth maps across all frames and rasterize the aggregated points in the world frame to obtain a partial background panorama Iₚₐₙₒᵖᵃʳᵗⁱᵃˡ. Next, we apply single-camera calibration [(Veicht et al., 2024)] to align the panorama with the gravity direction and use a panorama diffusion outpainting model [(nomadoor, 2026; Labs, 2025a)] to generate a complete 360^∘ background panorama Iₚₐₙₒ^full. Finally, a panorama-to-3D model [(Team HY-World, 2026; Labs, 2025b)] lifts it into background Gaussians G_bgʷᵒʳˡᵈ.

Dynamic Foreground Generation. We generate a dynamic Gaussian representation for each foreground object conditioned on its visible pixels in the input video. Dynamic object modeling remains an active area of research [(Sabathier et al., 2026; Liao et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026b; Yenphraphai et al., 2026)], with visual backbones offering different capabilities across motion types. We therefore adopt a unified formulation with motion-type-specific instantiations for three categories: rigid-body motion, which preserves object shape; human motion, which includes body articulation; and general deformable motion, which allows flexible shape changes without assuming a human body model. Across all three types, we model global motion through per-frame scale, rotation, and translation, while treating local deformation differently.

Generation comprises two shared components: i) Object Motion Estimation: For each foreground object i and frame t, we estimate a similarity transformation H_i,t^obj→cam=(α_i,t,R_i,t,p_i,t)∈Sim(3), where α_i,t, R_i,t, and p_i,t denote scale, rotation, and translation, respectively. This transformation maps the object’s locally deformed geometry from object space into camera space at frame t. These parameters describe its scale, orientation, and position, while local shape changes are modeled by the second component, described next.

ii) Deformable Gaussian Generation: Conditioned on visible foreground pixels of object i, we generate its canonical Gaussians Gᵢᵒᵇʲ and a time-dependent deformation field Φ_i,t. This field maps Gᵢᵒᵇʲ to their deformed configuration in object space at frame t, capturing local articulation or shape changes, and reduces to the identity for rigid objects. We apply Φ_i,t, followed by the object-to-camera transformation H_i,t^obj→cam and the camera-to-world transformation Tₜ^c→w, to obtain dynamic foreground Gaussians G_i,tʷᵒʳˡᵈ. The full formulation and motion-type-specific instantiations are provided in Appendix (Sec. A). The resulting foreground Gaussians and object trajectories are then aligned with the panoramic background.

Foreground-Background Alignment. Since the foreground and background are generated independently, their scales and local geometry may be inconsistent. We align the independently generated foreground and background through global scale alignment and local displacement correction. We first estimate a background scale s in closed form by matching the generated background to the video-derived point cloud over their common visible region. For each foreground object, we then estimate displacements δ_i,t from correspondences between its local contact neighborhood and the scale-aligned background. For frames without reliable contact, we interpolate the displacements from supported frames, retaining the nearest displacement outside their temporal range. We apply these corrections to the object’s world-space positions, p_i,tʷᵒʳˡᵈ+δ_i,t, and its Gaussians to obtain an aligned 4D visual scene. Details are provided in Appendix (Sec. B).

4.3 Dynamic Spatial Sound Field Generation via Diffusion Synchronization

The reconstructed 4D visual scene provides the geometry and trajectories of sound sources, while the video provides their semantic and temporal context. Our goal is to generate persistent source signals that can be spatially re-rendered along arbitrary listener trajectories while remaining consistent with the acoustic events observed in the input video.

To this end, we represent audio in two complementary spaces. We denote by aᶜᵃᵐ a video-conditioned camera-space mixture, which captures the overall acoustic content observed by the input camera, and by aᵢᵒᵇʲ the object-space signal of dynamic source i∈I_dyn, which can be independently re-rendered from novel listener poses. Generating these signals independently, however, does not guarantee that the object tracks explain the camera-space mixture. We therefore couple the two representations through the acoustic renderer induced by the reconstructed 4D scene.

Static Background Sound Generation. We generate background audio using the VLM-derived descriptions and grounding labels obtained during video preprocessing. For each static source, a text-to-audio model [(Shan et al., 2025)] synthesizes a source signal conditioned on its textual description. To spatially ground the signal, we use its grounding label to prompt SAM3 [(Carion et al., 2026)] for segmentation in the background panorama and associate the resulting region with the reconstructed background geometry, obtaining a point cloud as a fixed spatial anchor for the source. Global ambience is maintained as a separate, non-spatialized background track. Together, the rendered static-source signals and ambience provide the background contribution a_staticᶜᵃᵐ to the camera-space mixture used for diffusion synchronization (Eq. 4).

Bidirectional Camera-Object Consistency. For each dynamic source i∈I_dyn, the reconstructed scene defines an acoustic rendering operator ℝᵢ that maps its object-space signal to its contribution along the observed camera trajectory. We focus on outdoor scenes with limited reverberation and model direct-path propagation with Doppler shifts, distance attenuation, and air absorption, omitting reflected paths. Rendering and summing the source tracks gives a camera-space prediction:

ãᶜᵃᵐ=∑_i∈I_dynℝᵢ (aᵢᵒᵇʲ)+aᶜᵃᵐ_static,

(4)

where aᶜᵃᵐ_static denotes the rendered static-source and ambient contributions. We require this rendered mixture to remain consistent with the video-conditioned prediction aᶜᵃᵐ.

Conversely, the camera-space mixture provides a video-aligned cue for each dynamic source. We first isolate source i using a query-conditioned separator Sep_qᵢ and then approximately invert its acoustic propagation:

ãᵢᵒᵇʲ=ℚᵢ (Sep_qᵢ (aᶜᵃᵐ)),

(5)

where qᵢ is the source-specific separation prompt and Sep(·) is instantiated with SAM-Audio [(Shi et al., 2025)]. Here, ℚᵢ is the inverse renderer that maps the separated camera-space signal back to object space. Together, Eqs. 4 and 5 establish bidirectional camera–object consistency, applying the object-space constraint. Static and ambient tracks contribute to the forward camera-space mixture but do not receive camera-to-object synchronization feedback. We detail the complete inverse formulation and its derivation in the Appendix (Sec. D).

Dual-Space Diffusion Synchronization. We enforce the above constraints during sampling by synchronizing one camera-space diffusion trajectory with the object-space trajectories of all dynamic sources. We use the flow-matching formulation of HY-VideoFoley [(Shan et al., 2025)]. At each flow step, we first predict clean audio for every branch, synchronize the predictions in audio space through Eq. 4 and Eq. 5, and then map the synchronized predictions back to the latent flow.

Clean prediction. Let τ∈[0,1) denote flow time, and let z_τᵏ and v_τᵏ denote the latent state and predicted velocity of branch k, where k∈{cam}∪I_\rmdyn. We extrapolate each branch to its predicted clean endpoint and decode it with the audio decoder Dec:

ẑ_1|τᵏ=z_τᵏ+(1-τ)v_τᵏ, â_τᵏ=Dec (ẑ_1|τᵏ).

(6)

Audio-space synchronization. We first render the object-space predictions into camera space:

ã_τᶜᵃᵐ=∑_i∈I_dynℝᵢ(â_i,τᵒᵇʲ)+a_staticᶜᵃᵐ.

(7)

We synchronize the camera-space prediction using

ā_τᶜᵃᵐ=(1-η_cam)â_τᶜᵃᵐ+η_camã_τᶜᵃᵐ, η_cam∈[0,1].

(8)

Conversely, the camera-space prediction provides an object-space hint ã_i,τᵒᵇʲ=ℚᵢ(Sep_qᵢ(â_τᶜᵃᵐ)). The synchronized object-space target is then

ā_i,τᵒᵇʲ=(1-η_obj)â_i,τᵒᵇʲ+η_objã_i,τᵒᵇʲ, η_obj∈[0,1].

(9)

Synchronized flow update. We encode each synchronized audio target into a clean latent endpoint z̄_1|τᵏ=Enc (ā_τᵏ), and replace the branch velocity by the direction toward this synchronized endpoint:

v_sync,τᵏ=(z̄_1|τᵏ-z_τᵏ)/(1-τ), (dz_τᵏ)/(dτ)=v_sync,τᵏ.

(10)

Repeating this procedure throughout sampling couples the video-conditioned camera trajectory with the object-conditioned source trajectories, producing source signals that remain both video-consistent and independently re-renderable.

4.4 Free-Viewpoint Rendering of Dynamic Scenes

Given a target camera/listener trajectory pₜ=[Rₜ,xₜ]∈SE(3), we render the visual and audio streams in the same world coordinate system. For visuals, we render the static background and dynamic foreground objects at time t using the reconstructed Gaussian splats, compositing the foreground objects according to their estimated trajectories Xᵢ(t). For audio, we first render each localized source signal into the listener coordinate frame using the acoustic renderer, which accounts for source position, motion, attenuation, and visibility. The resulting directional source contributions are then encoded into ambisonics:

a_L(t)=∑_i∈I_dyn∪I_staticσᵢ(t) aᵢ(tᵢᵉᵐ) y_L (Rₜ^⊤(sᵢ(t)-xₜ)/(∥sᵢ(t)-xₜ∥)),

(11)

where I_dyn and I_static index dynamic foreground sources and localized static background sources, respectively, and aᵢ denotes the corresponding source signal. The world-space source position sᵢ(t) follows the reconstructed trajectory for dynamic sources and remains fixed for static sources. Here, tᵢᵉᵐ is the emission time, σᵢ(t) models distance attenuation and occlusion, and y_L denotes spherical harmonics up to order L. Finally, the ambisonics signal is decoded to binaural audio with an HRTF decoder:

b(t)=∑_ℓ=0^L∑_m=-ℓ^ℓh_ℓ,m⋆a_ℓ,m(t),

(12)

where h_ℓ,m are the left/right HRIR filters for each ambisonics channel. Global ambience is then mixed with b(t) to produce the final binaural output. This produces synchronized novel-view video and listener-dependent spatial audio along the target trajectory.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experiment Settings

We evaluate on our newly collected dataset, SonoScene4D, with metrics introduced in Sec. 3, by rendering spatial audio at the microphone pose and comparing it with the ground-truth FOA recording. We compare against four prior methods that generate spatial audio from visual inputs:

  • •

    ViSAGe[(Kim et al., 2025)]: generates ambisonics at the input camera pose from a field-of-view (FoV) video, without supporting novel-view audio rendering. To evaluate it at the target microphone pose, we provide a FoV video rendered from our 4D visual scene at that pose.

  • •

    OmniAudio[(Liu et al., 2025a)]: generates ambisonics at the input camera pose from a panoramic video, likewise without supporting novel-view audio rendering. We therefore provide a panoramic video rendered from our 4D visual scene at the target microphone pose.

  • •

    SonoWorld[(Jin et al., 2026)]: generates a static 3D audio-visual scene from a single image. Since it does not model scene dynamics, we use the middle frame of the input video and otherwise follow its original setting for evaluation.

  • •

    Sonic4D[(Xie et al., 2025)]: is the closest prior method for spatializing video-conditioned monaural audio in 4D scenes. It supports novel-view rendering but assumes a single sound source. We retain its visual backbone and audio pipeline, track the dominant moving sound source, and render at the target microphone pose. For comparison with ground-truth FOA, we adapt its binaural renderer using one omnidirectional and three co-located, orthogonal figure-eight virtual microphones.

    • We also compare with two variants of our method: Ours (T2A), which uses text-to-audio generation for each dynamic-source track, and Ours (V2A), which instead uses video-to-audio generation conditioned on the input video.

    5.2 Quantitative Results

    Quantitative Evaluation on SonoScene4D. Tab. 1 shows results on Video-to-4DAVScene using the metrics defined in Sec. 3. Compared with prior video-to-audio generation baselines, including ViSAGe[(Kim et al., 2025)] and OmniAudio[(Liu et al., 2025a)], SonoWorld4D achieves substantially better performance. Compared with SonoWorld and Sonic4D[(Xie et al., 2025)], we also show large gains, confirming the effectiveness of our explicit object-space audio generation and dual-space synchronization mechanisms, which improve spatial audio consistency over a trajectory-based dynamic spatialization baseline.

    User Study. We conduct a user study with 50 participants comparing our method against baselines and ablated variants across nine dynamic scenes from our dataset and web videos, covering multi-source scenarios and rigid-body, human, and general deformable motion. Participants use headphones to assess audio-visual synchronization, spatial direction and distance cues, audio quality, and consistency with a shared sound source description. Comparisons with Sonic4D also assess overall visual quality. As shown in Fig. 5, participants prefer our audio over OmniAudio and Sonic4D in 94.0% and 66.4% of comparisons, respectively, and our visuals over Sonic4D in 89.8%. Our full method is also preferred over the T2A and V2A variants in 90.7% and 70.7% of audio comparisons, respectively. See appendix (Sec. F) for details.

    5.3 Qualitative Results

    Time-Azimuth RMS Visualization. Fig. 3 visualizes time–azimuth RMS maps of generated ambisonics for scenes in SonoScene4D, alongside reference FOA recordings at the target microphone poses. Brighter regions indicate stronger directional responses. Our maps more closely follow the reference patterns across both vehicle and human scenes. In vehicle scenes, the bright bands track the changing sound direction as vehicles move through the scene; in human scenes, the maps retain intermittent responses aligned with repeated acoustic events. The baselines exhibit misplaced directional responses, overly persistent bands, or reduced temporal variation, confirming that our method better captures both the evolving sound directions and the temporal structure.

    Novel-Listener Audio Adaptation. Fig. 4 further visualizes audio generated for a novel listener position in the airplane scene, alongside the input video and our novel-view visual renderings. Intervals (a) and (b) indicate when the airplane is closest to the input camera and the novel listener, respectively. At the novel listener position, the strongest response should occur near (b), with frequencies shifting downward as the airplane passes. Sonic4D retains a strong response near (a). Ours (V2A) responds near both intervals, as its generated audio already encodes Doppler shifts and loudness variations tied to the input camera position, which persist when re-rendered for the novel listener. Ours (T2A) responds near (b) but with less distinct spectral structure. Our full method produces a dominant response and a clear downward frequency shift around (b), consistent with the expected Doppler effect. These results confirm that the synchronization scheme effectively adapts both the amplitude envelope and motion-dependent frequency content to the novel listener position.

    6 Conclusion

    We presented Video-to-4DAVScene, a new task that transforms a monocular video into an explorable, time-varying 4D audio-visual scene, and SonoWorld4D, a training-free framework for this task. Our framework combines a 4D visual scene representation that decomposes scenes into static backgrounds and dynamic foreground objects in a unified world coordinate system, with a novel diffusion synchronization mechanism tailored for dynamic spatial sound field generation. This enables real-time interactive exploration with moving sound sources and temporally, semantically, and geometrically aligned visual and spatial audio rendering. Experiments on real-world dynamic scenes demonstrate that SonoWorld4D outperforms a series of baselines on both objective metrics and in a user study. Future work will explicitly model object materials to support more physically accurate rendering of interaction-driven sounds in dynamic scenes.

    Acknowledgments

    This work was supported in part by faculty research awards from Sony and Dolby Laboratories and by the Barry Mersky and Capital One Endowed Professorships.

    AI use statement

    We used AI tools to refine author-written text and assist with code development for this work. The authors reviewed and revised the AI-assisted text and code and take full responsibility for the final manuscript and implementation.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix

    Appendix A Motion-Type-Specific Instantiations for Dynamic Foreground Generation

    Our dynamic foreground generation follows the same two components for all motion types: Object Motion Estimation, which estimates the global similarity transformation H_i,t^obj→cam from object space to camera space at each frame, and Deformable Gaussian Generation, which produces canonical Gaussians Gᵢᵒᵇʲ and their time-dependent deformation Φ_i,t. We instantiate these components with different backbones for rigid-body, human, and general deformable motion, while retaining the shared formulation:

    G_i,tʷᵒʳˡᵈ=Tₜ^c→w[(H_i,t^obj→cam∘Φ_i,t)(Gᵢᵒᵇʲ)].

    		(13)

    Fig. 6 summarizes how each motion type instantiates these two components. All outputs are subsequently aligned with the panoramic background through the foreground-background alignment described in the main paper.

    A.1 Rigid-Body Motion

    Object Motion Estimation. We use MV-SAM3D [(Li et al., 2026)] to jointly reconstruct a proxy mesh and canonical Gaussians from selected frames of the input video. Using this mesh, FoundationPose [(Wen et al., 2024)] estimates object rotation and translation through anchor-frame registration and temporal tracking. We complete motion estimates across unreliable or missing observations using trajectory interpolation and extrapolation. Together with reconstruction-derived scale estimates, the resulting poses specify H_i,t^obj→cam. Keyframe selection, tracking, and trajectory completion are detailed in Appendix G.2.

    Deformable Gaussian Generation. We use the canonical Gaussians Gᵢᵒᵇʲ jointly produced with the proxy mesh by MV-SAM3D. Reconstruction is conditioned on foreground images, masks, and depth-derived pointmaps from selected keyframes. Since rigid objects preserve their shape, we set Φ_i,t=Id and reuse the same canonical Gaussians throughout the sequence.

    A.2 Human Motion

    Object Motion Estimation. We use GEM  [(Li et al., 2025)] to recover SMPL-X  [(Pavlakos et al., 2019)] parameters from the foreground video, including global body motion and articulated poses. The global body pose provides the rotation and translation needed for H_i,t^obj→cam. We reconcile the human reconstruction with the scene scale using the ratio between predicted scene depth and rendered human depth over foreground pixels. The camera poses from video preprocessing then map the recovered motion into the common world frame.

    Deformable Gaussian Generation. We use LHM++  [(Qiu et al., 2025)] to reconstruct an animatable Gaussian avatar from reference images of the person. The avatar provides Gᵢᵒᵇʲ, and skeletal skinning driven by the estimated SMPL-X pose sequence instantiates Φ_i,t. This captures body articulation while maintaining a shared appearance representation across frames.

    A.3 General Deformable Motion

    Object Motion Estimation. We use SAM3D [(Team et al., 2025)] to reconstruct a proxy mesh for each frame, conditioned on the foreground image, mask, and depth-derived pointmap. We use these per-frame meshes with FoundationPose [(Wen et al., 2024)] to estimate object rotation and translation through pose registration and tracking. Allowing the proxy geometry to vary across frames accounts for the object’s changing shape. Together with reconstruction-derived scale estimates, the resulting poses specify H_i,t^obj→cam.

    Deformable Gaussian Generation. We initialize the canonical Gaussians Gᵢᵒᵇʲ from the SAM3D reconstruction of a reference frame and use Lift4D [(Litman et al., 2026)] to fit the time-dependent deformation field Φ_i,t to the per-frame reconstructions and observed foreground images. The deformation field is parameterized by learned control nodes, supporting non-human articulation and flexible shape changes without assuming a human body model. We combine the deformed Gaussians with the estimated object-to-camera transformations using the same formulation as the other two instantiations.

    Appendix B Details on Foreground-Background Alignment

    Foreground reconstruction and panorama-to-3D generation produce geometry independently. Although their coordinate orientations are established by camera estimation and panorama calibration, their scales and local surfaces may disagree. We address these discrepancies through a scene-level background scale followed by time-varying foreground displacement corrections.

    B.1 Global Scale Alignment

    We render the video-derived background point cloud and the generated background Gaussians into the same panoramic view. Let dᵢₙᵢₜ(u) and d_bg(u) denote their radial depths at panorama pixel u, respectively. We retain reliable correspondences over their common visible region, denoted by U, and weight them by observation confidence wᵤ=C_obs(u).

    We estimate a single scene-level background scale through weighted least squares:

    s=\undersets̃>0\arg\min∑_u∈Uwᵤ(s̃ d_bg(u)-dᵢₙᵢₜ(u))²=(∑_u∈Uwᵤ d_bg(u)dᵢₙᵢₜ(u))/(∑_u∈Uwᵤ d_bg(u)²).

    		(14)

    We apply this scale to the generated background geometry and map it into the common world frame using the known panorama-to-world transformation.

    B.2 Local Displacement Estimation

    Global scale alignment does not resolve local geometric differences between the two reconstructions. For each object i and frame t, we collect background points in a neighborhood of its foreground mask M_i,t. We exclude foreground pixels and use depth and surface-normal discontinuities to restrict the neighborhood to connected geometry. For supported objects, such as a car on a road, this neighborhood captures the nearby supporting surface.

    We project these points into the reference panorama and retain correspondences that are visible and depth-consistent with the initialized background, with valid geometry in the generated background. For each retained correspondence p, let x_i,t,p be the video-derived point and y_i,t,p its corresponding point on the scale-aligned background, both in world space. Their displacement is Δx_i,t,p=y_i,t,p-x_i,t,p.

    After rejecting displacement outliers, we estimate the local translation by a weighted average:

    δ̂_i,t=(∑_p∈Ω_i,tw_i,t,p Δx_i,t,p)/(∑_p∈Ω_i,tw_i,t,p),

    		(15)

    where Ω_i,t is the retained support set and w_i,t,p combines depth confidence with background rendering opacity. We accept a displacement estimate only when its support is sufficient and its residual displacements are consistent.

    B.3 Displacement Interpolation

    Frames without reliable local support, such as an airborne interval, do not provide direct displacement constraints. We propagate the accepted estimates through a temporally regularized correction field. Let Tᵢ denote the supported frames and c_i,t the confidence of each accepted estimate. We solve

    \min_{δ_i,t}ₜ₌₁ᵀ∑_t∈Tᵢc_i,t ρ (∥δ_i,t-δ̂_i,t∥₂)+η∑ₜ₌₁ᵀ⁻¹∥δ_i,t+1-δ_i,t∥₂²,

    		(16)

    where ρ is a Huber penalty and η controls temporal smoothness.

    This optimization smooths the supported displacement estimates and linearly interpolates the resulting offsets across intervals without reliable contact. Outside the supported temporal range, the correction remains equal to the nearest supported offset. If no reliable support is available throughout the sequence, we set δ_i,t=0 and retain the original trajectory.

    Finally, we update each object’s world-space position as

    p̃_i,tʷᵒʳˡᵈ=p_i,tʷᵒʳˡᵈ+δ_i,t,

    		(17)

    and apply the same translation to its Gaussians, preserving object rotations and local deformations. Together with the scale-aligned background, these corrected foreground objects form the aligned 4D visual scene.

    Appendix C Ablation on Visual Components

    We examine two components of visual scene generation: the displacement correction in foreground-background alignment and the panorama-to-3D backbone used for background generation. Fig. 7 provides qualitative comparisons.

    Foreground-background displacement correction. We compare our full alignment, which combines global scale alignment with local displacement corrections, against a variant that retains only scale alignment. Global scale alone cannot resolve local geometric discrepancies between the independently reconstructed foreground and background. The scale-only variant places much of the car below the road surface. Adding displacement corrections substantially reduces this interpenetration and improves object-ground contact. This comparison illustrates the importance of accounting for local geometry in addition to global scale.

    Panorama-to-3D backbone. We compare HYWorld 2.0 [(Team HY-World, 2026)] and Marble [(Labs, 2025b)] for lifting the completed background panorama into 3D Gaussians. Both produce usable background reconstructions, demonstrating that our framework accommodates different panorama-to-3D backbones. In our qualitative comparisons, however, HYWorld 2.0 exhibits more visible artifacts, including distorted vegetation and spurious geometry, while Marble produces cleaner renderings. For reproducibility, we use HYWorld 2.0 for all quantitative evaluations. For improved visual quality, we use the proprietary Marble model in our qualitative comparisons and demos.

    Appendix D Forward and Inverse Acoustic Rendering

    This section details the forward renderer ℝᵢ and inverse renderer ℚᵢ used for diffusion synchronization, and explains how occlusion is handled during camera-to-object fusion.

    Direct-Path Propagation.

    Measurements of natural acoustics show that reverberation typically decays faster outdoors than indoors [(Traer and McDermott, 2016)]. Perceptual experiments further show that strong room-like reverberation can sound atypical for low-intensity outdoor sources [(Traer et al., 2021)]. Motivated by these observations, we adopt an outdoor-focused direct-path approximation and omit reflected paths and reverberation. Our renderer accounts for Doppler shifts, distance attenuation, and air absorption, which change the timing and amplitude of each source signal.

    For source i, let t denote reception time at the camera and u denote emission time in object space. We write the emission-time mapping as u=φᵢ(t)=tᵢᵉᵐ(t). This mapping is determined by the source and camera trajectories, and its local rate accounts for the Doppler shift. Let gᵢ(t)>0 denote the multiplicative gain accounting for distance attenuation and air absorption. On available, unoccluded reception intervals Ωᵢ, the forward renderer is

    (ℝᵢaᵢᵒᵇʲ)(t)=gᵢ(t) aᵢᵒᵇʲ (φᵢ(t)), t∈Ωᵢ.

    		(18)

    This expression describes the unoccluded direct path. Occluded intervals are excluded from inverse-rendering feedback, as described below.

    Inverse Rendering.

    Given the source and camera trajectories, we treat φᵢ and gᵢ as known. We assume that φᵢ is strictly increasing over the time range considered, so that each emission time has a unique corresponding reception time. The inverse renderer first reverses this time mapping and then divides out the propagation gain. For a separated camera-space signal bᵢ,

    (ℚᵢbᵢ)(u)=(bᵢ (φᵢ⁻¹(u)))/(gᵢ (φᵢ⁻¹(u))), u∈Uᵢ,

    		(19)

    where Uᵢ=φᵢ(Ωᵢ) is the corresponding set of valid emission times. Substituting Eq. 18 into Eq. 19 gives

    (ℚᵢℝᵢaᵢᵒᵇʲ)(u)=(gᵢ (φᵢ⁻¹(u))aᵢᵒᵇʲ (φᵢ (φᵢ⁻¹(u))))/(gᵢ (φᵢ⁻¹(u)))(20)
    =aᵢᵒᵇʲ(u), u∈Uᵢ.

    Thus, the continuous-time propagation model is analytically invertible on valid intervals when the time mapping is strictly increasing and the gain is nonzero. In discrete time, evaluating the warped signal requires resampling, which introduces numerical approximation errors. Source-separation errors further affect the object-space estimate obtained from a camera-space mixture.

    Occlusion Handling and Fusion.

    We do not apply inverse rendering to occluded intervals. Instead, we define a validity mask on the object-space timeline:

    mᵢ(u)=\begincases1,&u∈Uᵢ, 0,&otherwise.\endcases

    		(21)

    The mask associates each emission time with the visibility and availability of its corresponding camera-space observation.

    At diffusion step τ, we obtain the inverse target only on valid intervals:

    ã_i,τᵒᵇʲ(u)=[ℚᵢ (Sep_qᵢ (â_τᶜᵃᵐ))](u), u∈Uᵢ.

    		(22)

    The object-space fusion is then

    ā_i,τᵒᵇʲ(u)=\begincases(1-η_obj)â_i,τᵒᵇʲ(u)+η_objã_i,τᵒᵇʲ(u),&mᵢ(u)=1, [3.0pt] â_i,τᵒᵇʲ(u),&mᵢ(u)=0.\endcases

    		(23)

    Visible intervals therefore receive camera-to-object feedback, while occluded or unavailable intervals retain the object-space branch’s own prediction during fusion. This avoids attempting to recover source signals from intervals where their camera-space contributions cannot be reliably inverted.

    Appendix E Details on Our SonoScene4D Dataset

    We collect SonoScene4D to evaluate spatial audio generation at listener positions distinct from the input camera viewpoints. The dataset contains 54 dynamic scenes: 25 vehicle scenes and 29 human scenes, covering rigid-body motion and human articulation. Each scene includes a panoramic video and synchronized first-order ambisonic (FOA) audio recorded at a separate listening position. The dataset includes both single-source and multi-source scenarios, with 13 scenes containing two dynamic foreground sound sources.

    Vehicle scenes. We capture 25 vehicle scenes across three locations, featuring police vehicles, pickup trucks, sedans, and buses. These scenes cover different vehicle appearances and acoustic characteristics, with vehicles moving through the scene along different trajectories. Three scenes contain two vehicles, requiring the generated audio to account for multiple moving sources and their respective spatial cues. The remaining 22 scenes contain a single foreground vehicle.

    Human scenes. We capture 29 human scenes across three locations. Activities include walking, jogging, jumping, foot stomping, clapping, burpees, and clapping while walking. These activities produce footsteps, hand claps, and ground-contact sounds with distinct temporal patterns, enabling evaluation of both spatial audio and synchronization with visible actions. Ten scenes contain two people performing either the same activity or different activities, such as walking and jogging, or clapping and jogging. The remaining 19 scenes contain one person. Some recordings additionally include static background sounds, such as flowing water, providing mixtures of dynamic foreground events and persistent background audio.

    Together, these scenes cover diverse source motions, acoustic events, and overlapping sound sources. The FOA recordings provide reference audio at a listening position different from the input camera position, allowing us to evaluate spatial audio generation at novel listener positions. We follow the annotation and capture-device setup protocols of the SonoScene360 dataset in SonoWorld [(Jin et al., 2026)].

    For experiments on SonoScene4D, we use our captured full background panorama as input to panorama-to-3D generation. For each dynamic foreground sound source, we extract a perspective field-of-view (FoV) video from the recorded panoramic sequence using mask-based tracking. Specifically, per-frame foreground masks determine the viewing direction of a virtual camera, whose orientation is temporally smoothed to follow the source with a fixed FoV. We project the panoramic frames into these views to obtain the foreground video inputs to our method, producing one tracked FoV video per dynamic sound source.

    Appendix F Details on User Study

    Platform and scene selection. We hosted the questionnaire on Zoho Forms and recruited participants internationally through Prolific’s AI Taskers pool. The study included seven scenes from web videos: bird singing, horse riding, karate, tap dancing, an airplane, a sports car, and a running humanoid robot. Two additional scenes from SonoScene4D featured two cars traveling in opposite directions and two people clapping, respectively.

    Comparison design. For each of the nine scenes, we compared our method against Sonic4D [(Xie et al., 2025)] and OmniAudio [(Liu et al., 2025a)], yielding 18 baseline comparisons. We additionally compared our full method against the V2A and T2A variants on three scenes: the airplane, two people clapping, and tap dancing. This yielded six ablation comparisons and 24 video pairs in total.

    Questionnaire. Each pair was accompanied by a one-sentence sound source description specifying the main objects and activities the users are expected to hear. Methods were presented as Method 1 and Method 2, without revealing their identities. For every pair, participants answered the required question: “Which method, A or B, do you prefer overall in terms of spatial audio?” For comparisons against Sonic4D, they additionally answered: “Which method, A or B, has better overall visual quality?” This second question was included only for Sonic4D because it uses its own visual generation backbone; OmniAudio and our ablated variants share our novel-view visual renderings. Each question required selecting one of the two methods, yielding 24 audio judgments and nine visual judgments per participant.

    Appendix G Implementation Details

    G.1 Component-Wise Implementation

    Video preprocessing and scene understanding. We use VGGT-Ω[(Wang et al., 2026)] to estimate per-frame depth, camera intrinsics, and camera poses, and SAM3 [(Carion et al., 2026)] to segment and track foreground objects. For the tracked FoV videos in SonoScene4D, we retain the known virtual-camera intrinsics and rotations used during panorama-to-perspective projection, together with the predicted depth. We query Kimi K3 [(Team et al., 2026)] with uniformly sampled video frames to obtain structured scene descriptions, sound-source attributes, and generation and separation prompts. The VLM prompt is summarized in Fig. 8.

    Visual scene generation. For background generation, we aggregate the observed background geometry into a partial panorama and use GeoCalib [(Veicht et al., 2024)] for gravity alignment. We complete missing regions using FLUX.2 Klein 9B [(Labs, 2025a)] with a panorama-outpainting LoRA [(nomadoor, 2026)]. For SonoScene4D, we instead use the captured full background panoramas. We use HYWorld 2.0 [(Team HY-World, 2026)] for panorama-to-3D generation in quantitative evaluations and Marble [(Labs, 2025b)] for qualitative comparisons and demos.

    Foreground generation follows the motion-type-specific instantiations in Appendix A, with reconstruction and motion estimation details provided in Appendix G.2.

    Foreground-background alignment. We follow the alignment procedure described in Appendix B. For scale estimation, we reject outliers in the log-depth ratios of reliable background correspondences before confidence-weighted fitting. For outdoor scenes, scale estimation uses the lower half of the reference panorama. Local displacement estimation uses visible, depth-consistent correspondences and rejects outliers before averaging.

    Audio generation and grounding. We instantiate both the camera-space video-to-audio branch and the object-space text-to-audio branches with HunyuanVideo-Foley [(Shan et al., 2025)], using its XXL configuration. The camera-space branch receives the input video and the full-scene audio description. By default, each object-space branch is conditioned only on its source-specific text prompt. We additionally enable video conditioning only when the VLM scene analysis indicates that the source remains at an approximately constant distance from the input camera throughout the video. We use SAM-Audio-small [(Shi et al., 2025)] for query-conditioned source separation during camera-to-object synchronization. Each static background sound is generated through text-to-audio conditioning. For non-global static sources, SAM3 segments the corresponding regions in the background panorama, which are associated with reconstructed background geometry to obtain fixed spatial anchors. Dynamic sources are associated with their reconstructed object trajectories, and global ambience is retained as a separate background track.

    Both generation branches use 100 Euler steps with a step size of 0.01 and classifier-free guidance of 6.0. Camera-space fusion uses η_cam=0.8, while the object-space fusion uses η_obj=0.5. For numerical stability, the denominator in the synchronized velocity update is clamped to \max(1-τ,0.05). Each source-separation call uses 32 midpoint steps with a step size of 1/32, without classifier-free guidance. Separation results are recomputed at each synchronization step, with hint caching disabled. Generated audio is decoded at 48 kHz.

    G.2 Foreground Reconstruction and Motion Estimation

    Rigid-body keyframe selection. We select up to 10 reliable keyframes per object for MV-SAM3D reconstruction and FoundationPose registration. We exclude frames with empty or insufficiently large foreground masks, substantial occlusion, severe image-boundary truncation, or blurred foreground observations. Among the valid frames, we choose the one with the largest foreground mask as the reconstruction reference. The remaining keyframes are selected by farthest-point sampling based on object positions and frame timestamps to cover both spatial motion and time.

    Pose registration and trajectory completion. We register object poses at anchor frames using FoundationPose and track bidirectionally between consecutive anchors, averaging valid estimates from both directions. Before the first anchor and after the last anchor, we track backward and forward, respectively. Tracking stops when observations become unreliable due to occlusion, insufficient object size, or departure from the image. For rigid-body objects, we fill gaps between reliable poses by interpolating translations and rotations, and complete trajectories outside this range using constant-velocity translation extrapolation and the nearest reliable rotation. Available foreground masks provide additional position and depth cues, and we refine the completed trajectories using silhouette-containment and temporal constraints.

    Human representation. We store posed human Gaussians relative to the SMPL-X pelvis and retain the pelvis trajectory separately. This allows foreground-background alignment to adjust global placement without modifying the recovered articulation.

    G.3 VLM Prompt

    We jointly provide sampled video frames to the VLM to obtain structured scene and sound-source descriptions. The JSON response includes a static environment description, an indoor/outdoor label, a full-scene audio description, and source-specific attributes and prompts. Each sound source is assigned a visual grounding label, a target peak level, and a spatial type. Dynamic foreground sources additionally receive rigidity and support-surface labels, together with identifiers linking their generation and separation prompts to the corresponding reconstructed objects. The support-surface labels also guide the layered rendering described in Appendix G.5. Fig. 8 summarizes the prompt instructions.

    G.4 Interactive Viewer

    We implement the browser-based viewer using Three.js111https://threejs.org/ and the Spark Gaussian Splatting renderer222https://sparkjs.dev/. The viewer loads background Gaussian layers, canonical foreground Gaussians, object transformations, and per-frame deformation attributes. Rigid objects reuse their canonical Gaussians with time-dependent global transformations. For deformable objects, we additionally update Gaussian positions and, where available, rotations and scales from the exported deformation sequences. All objects share a playback timeline, which also controls audio playback and seeking. Users can follow recorded camera paths or navigate freely through the scene.

    Interactive audio playback uses the Web Audio API333https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Web_Audio_API. The listener’s position and orientation follow the viewing camera. Dynamic source positions follow their reconstructed trajectories, while static sources remain at their grounded background anchors. Each localized source is spatialized using HRTF-based panning with distance-dependent attenuation, updating its spatial cues as the source or listener moves. The spatialized source contributions are mixed with global ambience to produce binaural output.

    G.5 Layered Rendering

    We use layered rendering to address two types of incorrect foreground occlusion. First, inaccuracies in object poses and reconstructed supporting surfaces can leave parts of an object below the surface, making feet or wheels appear buried even after foreground-background alignment. Second, sky Gaussians reconstructed by Marble may lie closer to the viewer than distant foreground objects, causing the sky to incorrectly occlude them. We therefore separate the background into sky, supporting surfaces, and other scene geometry, and introduce a depth tolerance when compositing foreground objects against the sky and supporting surfaces. Other scene geometry, such as trees and walls, retains depth-based occlusion.

    Background layer construction. After alignment, we partition the background Gaussians into sky, supporting surfaces, and remaining background geometry. For outdoor scenes, we segment the sky in the background panorama using SAM3 and transfer its mask to Gaussians by projecting their centers into the panorama. Indoor scenes omit the sky layer.

    To identify supporting surfaces, we use the VLM-provided surface labels as SAM3 prompts and combine these semantic masks with contact geometry. We collect the lowest foreground Gaussian points along the aligned trajectories and identify nearby background Gaussians at compatible heights as contact seeds. The support region grows from these seeds along a nearest-neighbor graph subject to spatial and height continuity constraints. When the semantic mask agrees with the contact seeds, it restricts the region to the named surface near the trajectory. Objects labeled as unsupported, such as a plane flying through the sky, do not contribute contact seeds. All background Gaussians outside the sky and support regions form the remaining geometry layer, which retains potential occluders such as trees, pillars, and walls.

    Depth-aware compositing. The viewer renders three groups separately: foreground objects, sky and supporting surfaces, and the remaining background geometry. For each group, we render both color and an alpha-weighted view-depth image using the same splat ordering and blending. The groups are then composited per pixel.

    Let d_fg, dₛᵤₚ, and d_occ denote the rendered depths of the foreground, the combined support/sky group, and the remaining background geometry, respectively. Foreground visibility relative to the remaining background follows the usual depth comparison, d_fg

    Layered compositing complements the geometric alignment by correcting residual visibility artifacts at display time. It leaves the reconstructed Gaussian positions, object trajectories, and acoustic geometry unchanged.
