    Appendix

    Appendix A Motion-Type-Specific Instantiations for Dynamic Foreground Generation

    Our dynamic foreground generation follows the same two components for all motion types: Object Motion Estimation, which estimates the global similarity transformation H_i,t^obj→cam from object space to camera space at each frame, and Deformable Gaussian Generation, which produces canonical Gaussians Gᵢᵒᵇʲ and their time-dependent deformation Φ_i,t. We instantiate these components with different backbones for rigid-body, human, and general deformable motion, while retaining the shared formulation:

    G_i,tʷᵒʳˡᵈ=Tₜ^c→w[(H_i,t^obj→cam∘Φ_i,t)(Gᵢᵒᵇʲ)].

    		(13)

    Fig. 6 summarizes how each motion type instantiates these two components. All outputs are subsequently aligned with the panoramic background through the foreground-background alignment described in the main paper.

    A.1 Rigid-Body Motion

    Object Motion Estimation. We use MV-SAM3D [(Li et al., 2026)] to jointly reconstruct a proxy mesh and canonical Gaussians from selected frames of the input video. Using this mesh, FoundationPose [(Wen et al., 2024)] estimates object rotation and translation through anchor-frame registration and temporal tracking. We complete motion estimates across unreliable or missing observations using trajectory interpolation and extrapolation. Together with reconstruction-derived scale estimates, the resulting poses specify H_i,t^obj→cam. Keyframe selection, tracking, and trajectory completion are detailed in Appendix G.2.

    Deformable Gaussian Generation. We use the canonical Gaussians Gᵢᵒᵇʲ jointly produced with the proxy mesh by MV-SAM3D. Reconstruction is conditioned on foreground images, masks, and depth-derived pointmaps from selected keyframes. Since rigid objects preserve their shape, we set Φ_i,t=Id and reuse the same canonical Gaussians throughout the sequence.

    A.2 Human Motion

    Object Motion Estimation. We use GEM  [(Li et al., 2025)] to recover SMPL-X  [(Pavlakos et al., 2019)] parameters from the foreground video, including global body motion and articulated poses. The global body pose provides the rotation and translation needed for H_i,t^obj→cam. We reconcile the human reconstruction with the scene scale using the ratio between predicted scene depth and rendered human depth over foreground pixels. The camera poses from video preprocessing then map the recovered motion into the common world frame.

    Deformable Gaussian Generation. We use LHM++  [(Qiu et al., 2025)] to reconstruct an animatable Gaussian avatar from reference images of the person. The avatar provides Gᵢᵒᵇʲ, and skeletal skinning driven by the estimated SMPL-X pose sequence instantiates Φ_i,t. This captures body articulation while maintaining a shared appearance representation across frames.

    A.3 General Deformable Motion

    Object Motion Estimation. We use SAM3D [(Team et al., 2025)] to reconstruct a proxy mesh for each frame, conditioned on the foreground image, mask, and depth-derived pointmap. We use these per-frame meshes with FoundationPose [(Wen et al., 2024)] to estimate object rotation and translation through pose registration and tracking. Allowing the proxy geometry to vary across frames accounts for the object’s changing shape. Together with reconstruction-derived scale estimates, the resulting poses specify H_i,t^obj→cam.

    Deformable Gaussian Generation. We initialize the canonical Gaussians Gᵢᵒᵇʲ from the SAM3D reconstruction of a reference frame and use Lift4D [(Litman et al., 2026)] to fit the time-dependent deformation field Φ_i,t to the per-frame reconstructions and observed foreground images. The deformation field is parameterized by learned control nodes, supporting non-human articulation and flexible shape changes without assuming a human body model. We combine the deformed Gaussians with the estimated object-to-camera transformations using the same formulation as the other two instantiations.

    Appendix B Details on Foreground-Background Alignment

    Foreground reconstruction and panorama-to-3D generation produce geometry independently. Although their coordinate orientations are established by camera estimation and panorama calibration, their scales and local surfaces may disagree. We address these discrepancies through a scene-level background scale followed by time-varying foreground displacement corrections.

    B.1 Global Scale Alignment

    We render the video-derived background point cloud and the generated background Gaussians into the same panoramic view. Let dᵢₙᵢₜ(u) and d_bg(u) denote their radial depths at panorama pixel u, respectively. We retain reliable correspondences over their common visible region, denoted by U, and weight them by observation confidence wᵤ=C_obs(u).

    We estimate a single scene-level background scale through weighted least squares:

    s=\undersets̃>0\arg\min∑_u∈Uwᵤ(s̃ d_bg(u)-dᵢₙᵢₜ(u))²=(∑_u∈Uwᵤ d_bg(u)dᵢₙᵢₜ(u))/(∑_u∈Uwᵤ d_bg(u)²).

    		(14)

    We apply this scale to the generated background geometry and map it into the common world frame using the known panorama-to-world transformation.

    B.2 Local Displacement Estimation

    Global scale alignment does not resolve local geometric differences between the two reconstructions. For each object i and frame t, we collect background points in a neighborhood of its foreground mask M_i,t. We exclude foreground pixels and use depth and surface-normal discontinuities to restrict the neighborhood to connected geometry. For supported objects, such as a car on a road, this neighborhood captures the nearby supporting surface.

    We project these points into the reference panorama and retain correspondences that are visible and depth-consistent with the initialized background, with valid geometry in the generated background. For each retained correspondence p, let x_i,t,p be the video-derived point and y_i,t,p its corresponding point on the scale-aligned background, both in world space. Their displacement is Δx_i,t,p=y_i,t,p-x_i,t,p.

    After rejecting displacement outliers, we estimate the local translation by a weighted average:

    δ̂_i,t=(∑_p∈Ω_i,tw_i,t,p Δx_i,t,p)/(∑_p∈Ω_i,tw_i,t,p),

    		(15)

    where Ω_i,t is the retained support set and w_i,t,p combines depth confidence with background rendering opacity. We accept a displacement estimate only when its support is sufficient and its residual displacements are consistent.

    B.3 Displacement Interpolation

    Frames without reliable local support, such as an airborne interval, do not provide direct displacement constraints. We propagate the accepted estimates through a temporally regularized correction field. Let Tᵢ denote the supported frames and c_i,t the confidence of each accepted estimate. We solve

    \min_{δ_i,t}ₜ₌₁ᵀ∑_t∈Tᵢc_i,t ρ (∥δ_i,t-δ̂_i,t∥₂)+η∑ₜ₌₁ᵀ⁻¹∥δ_i,t+1-δ_i,t∥₂²,

    		(16)

    where ρ is a Huber penalty and η controls temporal smoothness.

    This optimization smooths the supported displacement estimates and linearly interpolates the resulting offsets across intervals without reliable contact. Outside the supported temporal range, the correction remains equal to the nearest supported offset. If no reliable support is available throughout the sequence, we set δ_i,t=0 and retain the original trajectory.

    Finally, we update each object’s world-space position as

    p̃_i,tʷᵒʳˡᵈ=p_i,tʷᵒʳˡᵈ+δ_i,t,

    		(17)

    and apply the same translation to its Gaussians, preserving object rotations and local deformations. Together with the scale-aligned background, these corrected foreground objects form the aligned 4D visual scene.

    Appendix C Ablation on Visual Components

    We examine two components of visual scene generation: the displacement correction in foreground-background alignment and the panorama-to-3D backbone used for background generation. Fig. 7 provides qualitative comparisons.

    Foreground-background displacement correction. We compare our full alignment, which combines global scale alignment with local displacement corrections, against a variant that retains only scale alignment. Global scale alone cannot resolve local geometric discrepancies between the independently reconstructed foreground and background. The scale-only variant places much of the car below the road surface. Adding displacement corrections substantially reduces this interpenetration and improves object-ground contact. This comparison illustrates the importance of accounting for local geometry in addition to global scale.

    Panorama-to-3D backbone. We compare HYWorld 2.0 [(Team HY-World, 2026)] and Marble [(Labs, 2025b)] for lifting the completed background panorama into 3D Gaussians. Both produce usable background reconstructions, demonstrating that our framework accommodates different panorama-to-3D backbones. In our qualitative comparisons, however, HYWorld 2.0 exhibits more visible artifacts, including distorted vegetation and spurious geometry, while Marble produces cleaner renderings. For reproducibility, we use HYWorld 2.0 for all quantitative evaluations. For improved visual quality, we use the proprietary Marble model in our qualitative comparisons and demos.

    Appendix D Forward and Inverse Acoustic Rendering

    This section details the forward renderer ℝᵢ and inverse renderer ℚᵢ used for diffusion synchronization, and explains how occlusion is handled during camera-to-object fusion.

    Direct-Path Propagation.

    Measurements of natural acoustics show that reverberation typically decays faster outdoors than indoors [(Traer and McDermott, 2016)]. Perceptual experiments further show that strong room-like reverberation can sound atypical for low-intensity outdoor sources [(Traer et al., 2021)]. Motivated by these observations, we adopt an outdoor-focused direct-path approximation and omit reflected paths and reverberation. Our renderer accounts for Doppler shifts, distance attenuation, and air absorption, which change the timing and amplitude of each source signal.

    For source i, let t denote reception time at the camera and u denote emission time in object space. We write the emission-time mapping as u=φᵢ(t)=tᵢᵉᵐ(t). This mapping is determined by the source and camera trajectories, and its local rate accounts for the Doppler shift. Let gᵢ(t)>0 denote the multiplicative gain accounting for distance attenuation and air absorption. On available, unoccluded reception intervals Ωᵢ, the forward renderer is

    (ℝᵢaᵢᵒᵇʲ)(t)=gᵢ(t) aᵢᵒᵇʲ (φᵢ(t)), t∈Ωᵢ.

    		(18)

    This expression describes the unoccluded direct path. Occluded intervals are excluded from inverse-rendering feedback, as described below.

    Inverse Rendering.

    Given the source and camera trajectories, we treat φᵢ and gᵢ as known. We assume that φᵢ is strictly increasing over the time range considered, so that each emission time has a unique corresponding reception time. The inverse renderer first reverses this time mapping and then divides out the propagation gain. For a separated camera-space signal bᵢ,

    (ℚᵢbᵢ)(u)=(bᵢ (φᵢ⁻¹(u)))/(gᵢ (φᵢ⁻¹(u))), u∈Uᵢ,

    		(19)

    where Uᵢ=φᵢ(Ωᵢ) is the corresponding set of valid emission times. Substituting Eq. 18 into Eq. 19 gives

    (ℚᵢℝᵢaᵢᵒᵇʲ)(u)=(gᵢ (φᵢ⁻¹(u))aᵢᵒᵇʲ (φᵢ (φᵢ⁻¹(u))))/(gᵢ (φᵢ⁻¹(u)))(20)
    =aᵢᵒᵇʲ(u), u∈Uᵢ.

    Thus, the continuous-time propagation model is analytically invertible on valid intervals when the time mapping is strictly increasing and the gain is nonzero. In discrete time, evaluating the warped signal requires resampling, which introduces numerical approximation errors. Source-separation errors further affect the object-space estimate obtained from a camera-space mixture.

    Occlusion Handling and Fusion.

    We do not apply inverse rendering to occluded intervals. Instead, we define a validity mask on the object-space timeline:

    mᵢ(u)=\begincases1,&u∈Uᵢ, 0,&otherwise.\endcases

    		(21)

    The mask associates each emission time with the visibility and availability of its corresponding camera-space observation.

    At diffusion step τ, we obtain the inverse target only on valid intervals:

    ã_i,τᵒᵇʲ(u)=[ℚᵢ (Sep_qᵢ (â_τᶜᵃᵐ))](u), u∈Uᵢ.

    		(22)

    The object-space fusion is then

    ā_i,τᵒᵇʲ(u)=\begincases(1-η_obj)â_i,τᵒᵇʲ(u)+η_objã_i,τᵒᵇʲ(u),&mᵢ(u)=1, [3.0pt] â_i,τᵒᵇʲ(u),&mᵢ(u)=0.\endcases

    		(23)

    Visible intervals therefore receive camera-to-object feedback, while occluded or unavailable intervals retain the object-space branch’s own prediction during fusion. This avoids attempting to recover source signals from intervals where their camera-space contributions cannot be reliably inverted.

    Appendix E Details on Our SonoScene4D Dataset

    We collect SonoScene4D to evaluate spatial audio generation at listener positions distinct from the input camera viewpoints. The dataset contains 54 dynamic scenes: 25 vehicle scenes and 29 human scenes, covering rigid-body motion and human articulation. Each scene includes a panoramic video and synchronized first-order ambisonic (FOA) audio recorded at a separate listening position. The dataset includes both single-source and multi-source scenarios, with 13 scenes containing two dynamic foreground sound sources.

    Vehicle scenes. We capture 25 vehicle scenes across three locations, featuring police vehicles, pickup trucks, sedans, and buses. These scenes cover different vehicle appearances and acoustic characteristics, with vehicles moving through the scene along different trajectories. Three scenes contain two vehicles, requiring the generated audio to account for multiple moving sources and their respective spatial cues. The remaining 22 scenes contain a single foreground vehicle.

    Human scenes. We capture 29 human scenes across three locations. Activities include walking, jogging, jumping, foot stomping, clapping, burpees, and clapping while walking. These activities produce footsteps, hand claps, and ground-contact sounds with distinct temporal patterns, enabling evaluation of both spatial audio and synchronization with visible actions. Ten scenes contain two people performing either the same activity or different activities, such as walking and jogging, or clapping and jogging. The remaining 19 scenes contain one person. Some recordings additionally include static background sounds, such as flowing water, providing mixtures of dynamic foreground events and persistent background audio.

    Together, these scenes cover diverse source motions, acoustic events, and overlapping sound sources. The FOA recordings provide reference audio at a listening position different from the input camera position, allowing us to evaluate spatial audio generation at novel listener positions. We follow the annotation and capture-device setup protocols of the SonoScene360 dataset in SonoWorld [(Jin et al., 2026)].

    For experiments on SonoScene4D, we use our captured full background panorama as input to panorama-to-3D generation. For each dynamic foreground sound source, we extract a perspective field-of-view (FoV) video from the recorded panoramic sequence using mask-based tracking. Specifically, per-frame foreground masks determine the viewing direction of a virtual camera, whose orientation is temporally smoothed to follow the source with a fixed FoV. We project the panoramic frames into these views to obtain the foreground video inputs to our method, producing one tracked FoV video per dynamic sound source.

    Appendix F Details on User Study

    Platform and scene selection. We hosted the questionnaire on Zoho Forms and recruited participants internationally through Prolific’s AI Taskers pool. The study included seven scenes from web videos: bird singing, horse riding, karate, tap dancing, an airplane, a sports car, and a running humanoid robot. Two additional scenes from SonoScene4D featured two cars traveling in opposite directions and two people clapping, respectively.

    Comparison design. For each of the nine scenes, we compared our method against Sonic4D [(Xie et al., 2025)] and OmniAudio [(Liu et al., 2025a)], yielding 18 baseline comparisons. We additionally compared our full method against the V2A and T2A variants on three scenes: the airplane, two people clapping, and tap dancing. This yielded six ablation comparisons and 24 video pairs in total.

    Questionnaire. Each pair was accompanied by a one-sentence sound source description specifying the main objects and activities the users are expected to hear. Methods were presented as Method 1 and Method 2, without revealing their identities. For every pair, participants answered the required question: “Which method, A or B, do you prefer overall in terms of spatial audio?” For comparisons against Sonic4D, they additionally answered: “Which method, A or B, has better overall visual quality?” This second question was included only for Sonic4D because it uses its own visual generation backbone; OmniAudio and our ablated variants share our novel-view visual renderings. Each question required selecting one of the two methods, yielding 24 audio judgments and nine visual judgments per participant.

    Appendix G Implementation Details

    G.1 Component-Wise Implementation

    Video preprocessing and scene understanding. We use VGGT-Ω[(Wang et al., 2026)] to estimate per-frame depth, camera intrinsics, and camera poses, and SAM3 [(Carion et al., 2026)] to segment and track foreground objects. For the tracked FoV videos in SonoScene4D, we retain the known virtual-camera intrinsics and rotations used during panorama-to-perspective projection, together with the predicted depth. We query Kimi K3 [(Team et al., 2026)] with uniformly sampled video frames to obtain structured scene descriptions, sound-source attributes, and generation and separation prompts. The VLM prompt is summarized in Fig. 8.

    Visual scene generation. For background generation, we aggregate the observed background geometry into a partial panorama and use GeoCalib [(Veicht et al., 2024)] for gravity alignment. We complete missing regions using FLUX.2 Klein 9B [(Labs, 2025a)] with a panorama-outpainting LoRA [(nomadoor, 2026)]. For SonoScene4D, we instead use the captured full background panoramas. We use HYWorld 2.0 [(Team HY-World, 2026)] for panorama-to-3D generation in quantitative evaluations and Marble [(Labs, 2025b)] for qualitative comparisons and demos.

    Foreground generation follows the motion-type-specific instantiations in Appendix A, with reconstruction and motion estimation details provided in Appendix G.2.

    Foreground-background alignment. We follow the alignment procedure described in Appendix B. For scale estimation, we reject outliers in the log-depth ratios of reliable background correspondences before confidence-weighted fitting. For outdoor scenes, scale estimation uses the lower half of the reference panorama. Local displacement estimation uses visible, depth-consistent correspondences and rejects outliers before averaging.

    Audio generation and grounding. We instantiate both the camera-space video-to-audio branch and the object-space text-to-audio branches with HunyuanVideo-Foley [(Shan et al., 2025)], using its XXL configuration. The camera-space branch receives the input video and the full-scene audio description. By default, each object-space branch is conditioned only on its source-specific text prompt. We additionally enable video conditioning only when the VLM scene analysis indicates that the source remains at an approximately constant distance from the input camera throughout the video. We use SAM-Audio-small [(Shi et al., 2025)] for query-conditioned source separation during camera-to-object synchronization. Each static background sound is generated through text-to-audio conditioning. For non-global static sources, SAM3 segments the corresponding regions in the background panorama, which are associated with reconstructed background geometry to obtain fixed spatial anchors. Dynamic sources are associated with their reconstructed object trajectories, and global ambience is retained as a separate background track.

    Both generation branches use 100 Euler steps with a step size of 0.01 and classifier-free guidance of 6.0. Camera-space fusion uses η_cam=0.8, while the object-space fusion uses η_obj=0.5. For numerical stability, the denominator in the synchronized velocity update is clamped to \max(1-τ,0.05). Each source-separation call uses 32 midpoint steps with a step size of 1/32, without classifier-free guidance. Separation results are recomputed at each synchronization step, with hint caching disabled. Generated audio is decoded at 48 kHz.

    G.2 Foreground Reconstruction and Motion Estimation

    Rigid-body keyframe selection. We select up to 10 reliable keyframes per object for MV-SAM3D reconstruction and FoundationPose registration. We exclude frames with empty or insufficiently large foreground masks, substantial occlusion, severe image-boundary truncation, or blurred foreground observations. Among the valid frames, we choose the one with the largest foreground mask as the reconstruction reference. The remaining keyframes are selected by farthest-point sampling based on object positions and frame timestamps to cover both spatial motion and time.

    Pose registration and trajectory completion. We register object poses at anchor frames using FoundationPose and track bidirectionally between consecutive anchors, averaging valid estimates from both directions. Before the first anchor and after the last anchor, we track backward and forward, respectively. Tracking stops when observations become unreliable due to occlusion, insufficient object size, or departure from the image. For rigid-body objects, we fill gaps between reliable poses by interpolating translations and rotations, and complete trajectories outside this range using constant-velocity translation extrapolation and the nearest reliable rotation. Available foreground masks provide additional position and depth cues, and we refine the completed trajectories using silhouette-containment and temporal constraints.

    Human representation. We store posed human Gaussians relative to the SMPL-X pelvis and retain the pelvis trajectory separately. This allows foreground-background alignment to adjust global placement without modifying the recovered articulation.

    G.3 VLM Prompt

    We jointly provide sampled video frames to the VLM to obtain structured scene and sound-source descriptions. The JSON response includes a static environment description, an indoor/outdoor label, a full-scene audio description, and source-specific attributes and prompts. Each sound source is assigned a visual grounding label, a target peak level, and a spatial type. Dynamic foreground sources additionally receive rigidity and support-surface labels, together with identifiers linking their generation and separation prompts to the corresponding reconstructed objects. The support-surface labels also guide the layered rendering described in Appendix G.5. Fig. 8 summarizes the prompt instructions.

    G.4 Interactive Viewer

    We implement the browser-based viewer using Three.js111https://threejs.org/ and the Spark Gaussian Splatting renderer222https://sparkjs.dev/. The viewer loads background Gaussian layers, canonical foreground Gaussians, object transformations, and per-frame deformation attributes. Rigid objects reuse their canonical Gaussians with time-dependent global transformations. For deformable objects, we additionally update Gaussian positions and, where available, rotations and scales from the exported deformation sequences. All objects share a playback timeline, which also controls audio playback and seeking. Users can follow recorded camera paths or navigate freely through the scene.

    Interactive audio playback uses the Web Audio API333https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Web_Audio_API. The listener’s position and orientation follow the viewing camera. Dynamic source positions follow their reconstructed trajectories, while static sources remain at their grounded background anchors. Each localized source is spatialized using HRTF-based panning with distance-dependent attenuation, updating its spatial cues as the source or listener moves. The spatialized source contributions are mixed with global ambience to produce binaural output.

    G.5 Layered Rendering

    We use layered rendering to address two types of incorrect foreground occlusion. First, inaccuracies in object poses and reconstructed supporting surfaces can leave parts of an object below the surface, making feet or wheels appear buried even after foreground-background alignment. Second, sky Gaussians reconstructed by Marble may lie closer to the viewer than distant foreground objects, causing the sky to incorrectly occlude them. We therefore separate the background into sky, supporting surfaces, and other scene geometry, and introduce a depth tolerance when compositing foreground objects against the sky and supporting surfaces. Other scene geometry, such as trees and walls, retains depth-based occlusion.

    Background layer construction. After alignment, we partition the background Gaussians into sky, supporting surfaces, and remaining background geometry. For outdoor scenes, we segment the sky in the background panorama using SAM3 and transfer its mask to Gaussians by projecting their centers into the panorama. Indoor scenes omit the sky layer.

    To identify supporting surfaces, we use the VLM-provided surface labels as SAM3 prompts and combine these semantic masks with contact geometry. We collect the lowest foreground Gaussian points along the aligned trajectories and identify nearby background Gaussians at compatible heights as contact seeds. The support region grows from these seeds along a nearest-neighbor graph subject to spatial and height continuity constraints. When the semantic mask agrees with the contact seeds, it restricts the region to the named surface near the trajectory. Objects labeled as unsupported, such as a plane flying through the sky, do not contribute contact seeds. All background Gaussians outside the sky and support regions form the remaining geometry layer, which retains potential occluders such as trees, pillars, and walls.

    Depth-aware compositing. The viewer renders three groups separately: foreground objects, sky and supporting surfaces, and the remaining background geometry. For each group, we render both color and an alpha-weighted view-depth image using the same splat ordering and blending. The groups are then composited per pixel.

    Let d_fg, dₛᵤₚ, and d_occ denote the rendered depths of the foreground, the combined support/sky group, and the remaining background geometry, respectively. Foreground visibility relative to the remaining background follows the usual depth comparison, d_fg

    Layered compositing complements the geometric alignment by correcting residual visibility artifacts at display time. It leaves the reconstructed Gaussian positions, object trajectories, and acoustic geometry unchanged.

item.title: 生成出来的 3D 场景得能被查询：LucidLyra 从前馈视频 latent 里直接给出语义与实例 ｜ LucidLyra: Feed-Forward Generative 3D Scene Reconstruction and Joint Understanding via Multi-Modal Latents
item.description:
一句话：物理 AI 与机器人要的不只是好看，还要「这是哪个物体」；这条让重建结果自带语义与身份。

要点：

  • 需求侧写得很直白：生成式 3D 重建能造出虚拟环境，但下游（机器人、物理 AI）不只需要视觉真实，还要能访问场景语义与物体身份
  • 现有 3D 理解方法要么依赖已采集的多视图场景、要么泛化有限、要么代价高
  • LucidLyra 用前馈方式从视频 latent 直接重建并「联合理解」：重建出的场景可被查询语义与实例，不需要额外标注流程

为什么值得看：「AI 生成的场景能不能直接被引擎当关卡用」，卡点常常是缺结构化信息（哪些是可交互物体、哪些是实例）。把语义与实例放进同一次前馈里，等于让生成资产天生带一份场景图。

中文摘要：生成式 3D 重建可以从单张图像合成虚拟环境，但机器人、物理 AI 等下游应用不只需要视觉真实，还需要访问场景的语义与物体身份。现有 3D 理解方法要么依赖已采集的多视图场景，要么泛化能力有限，要么需要昂贵的额外流程。LucidLyra 提出一个前馈框架：从视频 latent 出发，一边做生成式 3D 重建，一边联合理解场景，使重建结果可以直接被查询语义与实例——也就是让「生成的场景」自带一份可用的结构化描述，而不是只有几何与贴图。对把生成内容接进引擎的管线，这一步决定了资产能否直接参与逻辑与交互。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-29

本期推送：2026-11-02

LucidLyra: Feed-Forward Generative 3D Scene Reconstruction and Joint Understanding via Multi-Task Distillation

Abstract

We present LucidLyra, a framework that makes generatively reconstructed 3D scenes directly queryable for semantics and instances in a feed-forward manner from video latents. While generative 3D reconstruction can synthesize virtual environments from a single image, downstream applications in robotics and physical AI require not only visual realism but also access to scene semantics and object identities. Existing 3D understanding approaches, however, require captured multi-view scenes, have limited generalization capabilities, or rely on expensive per-scene processing and optimization. To bridge this gap, our method distills complementary knowledge from a camera-controlled video diffusion model and frozen 2D vision foundation models into a unified model to jointly infer 3D Gaussians encoding geometry, appearance, open-vocabulary semantics, and class-agnostic instance cues. The resulting scenes support novel-view rendering, open-vocabulary segmentation, and object grouping without per-scene optimization, while training requires neither manual 3D annotations nor captured multi-view data. Our method outperforms baselines combining state-of-the-art 3DGS segmentation approaches with generative 3D scene reconstruction on curated synthetic and real-image-conditioned benchmarks, while preserving reconstruction quality. Furthermore, our latent formulation naturally extends to monocular video, reconstructing structured dynamic 3D scenes across time. By turning renderable but unstructured outputs into queryable 3D worlds, LucidLyra enables downstream applications including 3D scene editing, 3D asset mining, and robotic simulation.

1 Introduction

Recent generative reconstruction methods can turn a single image into a renderable 3D environment. Building upon learned generative models, they can imagine content beyond the observed field of view and consolidate it into a scene that can be viewed from new perspectives [14, 72, 52, 85, 76, 2]. Generated 3D environments are promising for scalable content generation in interactive media, physical AI simulation, and industrial applications in engineering and manufacturing [16]. However, existing generated scene representations primarily capture geometry and appearance, while lacking an explicit understanding of their content. Downstream applications in embodied AI and physical simulation cannot interact with an collection of colored primitives; they require structured scene elements with semantic roles and discrete instance boundaries to support collision reasoning, physical manipulation, and interactive scene editing.

A natural solution might seem to generate an appearance-only scene first and recover semantic and instance representations post-hoc. However, this two-stage route breaks down in the single-view generative setting. Existing post-hoc methods either attach 2D foundation-model predictions to an existing reconstruction through per-scene optimization [67, 105, 87, 100], or jointly infer geometry and understanding from multiple captured views [117, 26, 88]. The former requires expensive scene-specific foundation model preprocessing and optimization. The latter relies on captured multi-view inputs and is constrained by the limited scale and domain diversity of multi-view training data. Neither route directly yields a structured 3D scene that has been generated from a single image.

Scaling these capabilities is not merely a matter of attaching a feature head to a reconstruction model. Generated regions lack paired ground-truth supervision, so estimated geometry, semantics, and object boundaries can drift and disagree across views. Predictions from 2D vision models compound this, as their semantics and masks are not guaranteed to be view-consistent. The central challenge is to turn complementary but imperfect generative and perceptual signals into a consistent 3D representation while balancing geometry, appearance, semantics, and instances without compromising generation quality. An integrated model should let semantic priors and geometry reinforce each other, rather than tagging an isolated reconstruction with semantic or object information.

We introduce LucidLyra, a framework that unifies feed-forward generative 3D reconstruction and scene understanding in an explicit Gaussian representation (Fig.1). Our central insight is that a video generator provides a unified foundation for structured 3D scene generation, serving both as the shared backbone and as the source of training data. Building on Lyra’s latent-to-Gaussian formulation [2], LucidLyra learns a 3D scene representation from camera-controlled video latents through multi-task distillation. Given a single input image, we denoise the corresponding video latents across camera trajectories, and process them through two parallel branches. The teacher branch decodes the latent into an RGB video and applies frozen vision-language, segmentation, and tracking foundation models to obtain semantic and instance supervision. The student branch incorporates vision cues of the input view into the video latents and directly maps the shared latent into a 3D Gaussian scene. We consolidate the teacher predictions across the generated views and distill them into persistent semantic and instance fields on the Gaussian primitives, jointly with geometry and appearance. A single shared representation can therefore support novel-view rendering, open-vocabulary segmentation, and object grouping. As an initial exploration toward generative 4D scene understanding, we also extend the formulation to monocular video inputs and predict semantics- and instance-aware dynamic 3D scenes. For this novel task, we introduce an evaluation protocol with benchmarks covering static scenes, real-image domain transfer, and dynamic scenes.

On our static LucidLyra-SDG benchmark, LucidLyra improves semantic mIoU and class-agnostic instance mTrackPR over the strongest comparable baseline by 31.7 and 9.8 percentage points, while maintaining reconstruction fidelity, with a modest PSNR gain of 0.53 dB over Lyra. More broadly, this formulation turns pretrained video generation into a scalable source of supervision for structured 3D learning, opening a path from renderable but unstructured outputs to queryable 3D worlds that downstream systems can reason about and interact with. In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    We introduce a unified generative 3D model that produces an explicit Gaussian scene representation with geometry, appearance, open-vocabulary semantic, and class-agnostic instance features from a single image in a feed-forward fashion.

  • •

    We develop a multi-task distillation strategy that transfers 2D generative, semantic, and object-level knowledge through aligned generated views into a consistent 3D representation. This enables task-specific training without captured multi-view data or manual 3D annotations, and avoids per-scene optimization at inference time.

  • •

    We jointly evaluate reconstruction and understanding on static and dynamic scenes. LucidLyra consistently outperforms two-stage baselines across optimization-based, mask-lifting, and feed-forward 3DGS segmentation methods, while maintaining novel-view reconstruction fidelity on static scenes with a small reconstruction trade-off on dynamic scenes. We further demonstrate downstream applications including robotic simulation, 3D scene editing, and 3D asset mining.

    • 2 Related Work

    From observed reconstruction to generative scene construction. Neural radiance fields [58] and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) [28] fit per-scene representations, while feed-forward methods amortize reconstruction across scenes to predict 3D Gaussians for novel-view synthesis [6, 110] or estimate dense depth and camera parameters [93, 54, 4]. Dynamic formulations underwent a similar evolution from per-sequence fitting [104, 103] to feed-forward estimation [53, 101, 32], yet all remain bounded by observed multi-view coverage. Generative methods relax this constraint by synthesizing unobserved content. Early works distill diffusion priors into per-scene optimizations or iterative view inpaintings [64, 19]. Multi-view generators synthesize dense video trajectories for downstream reconstruction [14, 74], with later extensions incorporating panoramic scaffolds, geometric alignment, or long-horizon expansion [92, 94, 18, 79, 54, 89]. However, generation and 3D reconstruction remain decoupled into different stages.

    A closer line to our setting couples generation directly with feed-forward 3D prediction. Recent methods decode video latents into Gaussians [52], embed Gaussian feature fields within video diffusion [76], directly generate explicit 3D representations [85, 77], or align generative image, video, and 3D latent spaces [47, 21, 15]. Lyra [2] self-distills a feed-forward Gaussian decoder from a camera-controlled video foundation model [72, 59], using synthetic multi-view video trajectories as both the latent input and the supervision target for static and dynamic 3D synthesis. We build upon Lyra’s scalable, latent-to-Gaussian formulation, extending its feed-forward output from raw geometry and appearance to joint language-grounded semantics and class-agnostic instances.

    From per-scene optimization to amortized 3D scene understanding. Early works predict semantics and instances from point clouds [65, 66, 9, 25], while subsequent methods lift open-vocabulary 2D foundation features onto reconstructed geometry [63, 23, 86] or embed language fields into neural representations [113, 36, 81, 29]. For 3DGS, several approaches optimize per-Gaussian language fields, aggregate 2D foundation features, or lift multi-view masks into object-aware representations [45, 100, 116, 67, 87, 31, 7, 105, 98, 78, 99]. Feed-forward methods amortize understanding across scenes, either by encoding pre-existing 3DGS reconstructions [50] or by jointly predicting geometry alongside semantic, panoptic, or instance structure from multi-view inputs [42, 117, 26, 88, 49, 40, 35, 43, 80, 84, 56, 107, 38, 111]. Generative understanding approaches synthesize observations for language-aware reconstruction, modular scene assembly, or driving-specific world models [55, 22, 106, 11]. Yet, these formulations remain confined to domain-specific priors or assume multiple posed observations.

    Existing approaches follow two main paradigms: augmenting a scene-specific reconstruction or jointly inferring geometry and segmentation from multi-view inputs. The former requires a pre-existing reconstruction, precluding single-view generation, while post-hoc lifting decouples semantics from geometry, leaving fusion vulnerable to cross-view inconsistencies. Crucially, both rely on an expensive preprocessing stage with a 2D vision foundation model. Feed-forward approaches jointly predict geometry and segmentation, but train on captured multi-view datasets with narrow domain coverage limiting generalization. LucidLyra instead unifies scene understanding with generative reconstruction. Conditioned on a single image, its amortized latent-to-Gaussian decoder jointly predicts geometry, appearance, language-aligned semantic features, and class-agnostic instance features in a single feed-forward pass, without prior 3D reconstructions, per-scene optimization, or post-hoc lifting. Distilling frozen foundation models on generated video eliminates the need for captured multi-view data or manual 3D annotations.

    3 Semantic- and Instance-Aware Generative 3D Reconstruction

    Given an input image I₀, LucidLyra generates a queryable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [28] scene representation whose primitives jointly encode geometry, appearance, language-aligned semantics, and class-agnostic instance identity. Rather than supervising reconstruction alone as in Lyra [2], we use the multi-view outputs of a camera-controlled video generator to construct aligned 2D semantic and instance targets using frozen vision foundation models and distill them into an explicit 3D representation via an amortized feed-forward decoder (Fig.2).

    3.1 Preliminaries: Lyra Generative 3D Reconstruction

    Lyra [2] amortizes 3D reconstruction by mapping camera-controlled video latents directly into 3D Gaussians. Given an image I₀ and V camera trajectories ℂ=(ℂ⁽¹⁾,…,ℂ^(V)), a video diffusion model V generates multi-view latents Z=(Z⁽¹⁾,…,Z^(V)), while camera rays are mapped to Plücker encodings E≡E(ℂ). A feed-forward decoder D^Lyra_3DGS predicts a 3DGS scene representation from these inputs:

    G=D^Lyra_3DGS(Z,E)={gᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N, gᵢ=(μᵢ,sᵢ,qᵢ,αᵢ,cᵢ),

    		(1)

    where each of N Gaussian primitives gᵢ parameterizes position μᵢ, scale sᵢ, rotation quaternion qᵢ, opacity αᵢ, and color cᵢ, renderable via differentiable splatting ℝ. The predicted Gaussians are aligned to the source-ray grid of the generated views across all trajectories.

    To learn this mapping without 3D supervision, Lyra compares two decodings of Z: for target camera ℂₖ, a frozen VAE decoder outputs a teacher image Iₖ=D_RGB(Zₖ), supervising the rendered prediction Îₖ=ℝ(G,ℂₖ) alongside depth targets. At inference time, sampled latents Z yield Gaussians encoding only geometry and appearance.

    3.2 Semantic and Instance Gaussian Decoder

    To equip Gaussians with semantic and instance awareness, we introduce additional conditioning using vision features of the input image and dedicated output heads. First, we supplement the video model latents Z with dense input image features F₀ extracted with C-RADIOv3 [69, 17, 70]. We align F₀ with Z through a learned linear projection to the latent feature dimension. Spatial interpolation matches F₀ to the latent token grid, and broadcasting replicates it across trajectories and latent time. Each latent-time slice is then modulated by a learned scalar weight shared across channels and a learned global gate before being added to the video and ray tokens. Next, the 3DGS decoder’s shared trunk fuses the multi-view tokens into features H={hᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N, where each feature corresponds to a source ray on the multi-view video latent grid. Two parallel heads map these shared features to complementary Gaussian attributes: the reconstruction head D_rec predicts geometry and appearance parameters gᵢ, while the understanding head D_seg jointly predicts a semantic descriptor fᵢˢᵉᵐ∈ℝ¹²⁸, an object-level instance embedding eᵢⁱⁿˢᵗ∈ℝ¹², and a part-level embedding eᵢᵖᵃʳᵗ∈ℝ⁴:

    G̃=D_3DGS(Z,E,F₀)={g̃ᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N, g̃ᵢ=[D_rec(hᵢ)∥D_seg(hᵢ)].

    		(2)

    The shared 3DGS decoder trunk and each task-specific head consist of seven Mamba-2 [10] layers followed by one Transformer [91] layer. Operating synchronously on the shared token grid attaches understanding fields directly to the co-located Gaussian gᵢ, bypassing post-hoc 2D-to-3D association. For camera ℂₖ, a differentiable renderer ℝ(G̃,ℂₖ) outputs rendered RGB Îₖ, semantic maps F̂ₖˢᵉᵐ, and instance maps F̂ₖⁱⁿˢᵗ via volumetric α-blending, and depth D̂ₖ by accumulating primitive center depths.

    3.3 Multi-Task 2D Feature Distillation

    We supervise the understanding fields using decoded video frames Iₖ and frozen 2D vision foundation models—class-agnostic segmentation, video tracking, and vision-language foundation models—generalizing RGB self-distillation to multi-task 2D feature distillation without 3D labels. To resolve cross-view feature jitter and mask inconsistency across imagined views, we first establish cross-view object tracks to associate observations and pool coherent semantic targets.

    Aligned instance targets. To associate objects across trajectories, we run SAM’s automatic mask generator on the shared first frame I₀, filter redundancies by coverage, and use the surviving masks to seed independent SAM2 propagations along each trajectory [34, 71]. The resulting class-agnostic instance tracklets Yₖⁱⁿˢᵗ preserve trajectory visibility while linking observations from the same initial object. Regions disoccluded late in a trajectory lacking a first-frame seed are excluded from instance supervision.

    Track-consistent semantic targets. The instance tracklets also let us aggregate semantic evidence across views. We use RADSeg [1] to extract dense features aligned with the SigLIP2 [90] image–text space for every decoded frame Iₖ. Storing its native 1 152-dimensional descriptor on every Gaussian is computationally prohibitive, therefore we compress this space with a projection network P_VL:ℝ¹¹⁵² →ℝ¹²⁸ for both image and text embeddings. The projector is trained over frozen SigLIP2 image and text embeddings, using the vanilla SigLIP training objective [109] on the LAION-2B [75] dataset and remains frozen afterwards. Within each camera trajectory, we pool projected features over all pixels and frames belonging to each SAM track and assign the resulting centroid to every track pixel. This yields semantic targets Yₖˢᵉᵐ, where track pooling suppresses view-dependent feature jitter.

    Joint multi-task objective. We initialize the shared trunk and reconstruction head D_rec from pretrained Lyra and initialize D_seg from scratch, training the entire Gaussian decoder while keeping all 2D teacher models and P_VL frozen. At target camera ℂₖ, rendered predictions (Îₖ,D̂ₖ,F̂ₖˢᵉᵐ,F̂ₖⁱⁿˢᵗ) are supervised against targets (Iₖ,Dₖ,Yₖˢᵉᵐ,Yₖⁱⁿˢᵗ) via

    L=L_rec+Lₛₑₘ+λᵢₙₛₜLᵢₙₛₜ.

    		(3)

    L_rec mirrors Lyra, combining photometric ℓ₂, LPIPS [112], depth, and opacity losses to preserve geometry during feature grounding. Schedules and hyperparameters are detailed in AppendixA.

    Instance distillation. We learn a class-agnostic instance representation via supervised contrastive learning [30] over tracked pixels across views. For a sample u∈S at pixel pᵤ in view kᵤ with normalized embedding ēᵤ=norm₂(F̂_kᵤⁱⁿˢᵗ(pᵤ)), we define positive matches sharing track ID as ℙ(u)={v∈S∖{u}|Y_kᵥⁱⁿˢᵗ(pᵥ)=Y_kᵤⁱⁿˢᵗ(pᵤ)}. Over valid anchors U={u∈S||ℙ(u)|>0}, we optimize

    Lᵢₙₛₜ=-(1)/(|U|)∑_u∈U(1)/(|ℙ(u)|)∑_v∈ℙ(u)\log(\exp(ēᵤ^⊤ēᵥ/τᵢₙₛₜ))/(∑_a∈S∖{u}\exp(ēᵤ^⊤ēₐ/τᵢₙₛₜ)),

    		(4)

    with temperature τᵢₙₛₜ>0. This pulls rendered embeddings of the same tracked object together across views while repelling different objects, clustering the underlying 3D Gaussians into distinct instance fields. For part-level supervision, we apply the same objective in parallel to the part embeddings, defining positive and negative pairs from sub-object tracklet IDs within each object tracklet.

    Semantic distillation. We supervise rendered semantic features with pooled teacher descriptors. For rendered feature f̂≡F̂ₖˢᵉᵐ(p) and target y≡Yₖˢᵉᵐ(p) with ℓ₂-normalized counterparts f̂̄ and ȳ, we define the pointwise loss

    ℓₛₑₘ(f̂,y)=-1/2\log ((1+f̂̄^⊤ȳ)/(2)+ε_ℓ)+1/2dₛₑₘ\lVertf̂̄-ȳ\rVert₁,

    		(5)

    with dₛₑₘ=$128$. The cosine term aligns predictions with the SigLIP2 image–text space, while the ℓ₁ term refines coordinate-level precision. Averaging over rendered pixels yields Lₛₑₘ^2D. Rendered feature losses constrain a blend of several Gaussian features, rather than each primitive individually. We therefore additionally supervise each primitive directly: each Gaussian g̃ᵢ originates from an input ray (kᵢ,pᵢ), allowing us to penalize discrepancy against teacher target Y_kᵢˢᵉᵐ(pᵢ) as Lₛₑₘ^G, yielding the total semantic loss Lₛₑₘ=λₛₑₘ^2DLₛₑₘ^2D+λₛₑₘ^GLₛₑₘ^G.

    3.4 Inference: Querying the Generated Scene

    Given generated video latents, our Gaussian decoder predicts the scene G̃ in a single forward pass. Its per-Gaussian semantic and instance features enable open-vocabulary queries and object grouping directly in 3D, without using the distillation teachers or lifting predictions from 2D views.

    Open-vocabulary semantics. Given categorical text queries ℚ={s_c}_c=1^C, the frozen SigLIP2 text encoder Φ_T and projection network P_VL yield normalized embeddings t̄_c=norm₂(P_VL(Φ_T(s_c))). Each Gaussian g̃ᵢ is assigned to the category c^* that maximizes the cosine similarity with its primitive descriptor:

    c^∗=\arg\max_c∈{1,…,C}norm₂(fᵢˢᵉᵐ)^⊤t̄_c.

    		(6)

    Querying new vocabularies needs only text–Gaussian dot products without regeneration.

    Instance grouping. Within each predicted semantic class, we spatially smooth instance embeddings and cluster high-opacity Gaussians via HDBSCAN [5]. Unclustered Gaussians inherit instance IDs from their nearest neighbor in joint embedding and 3D space. For the part-level instance segmentation, we apply the same technique within each object cluster (cf. SectionA.3).

    LucidLyra+. Our optional semantic refinement leaves geometry and appearance unchanged. It uses a single RADSeg+ open-vocabulary prediction of I₀ as a 2D anchor, obtained at minimal overhead since RADSeg+ uses the same C-RADIO features. Our ray-aligned decoder grid links each anchor pixel to its corresponding Gaussian. For every well-supported anchor, we average the semantic features of its Gaussians into a prototype, and relabel any Gaussian whose feature is close enough to that prototype. All remaining Gaussians keep their original semantic labels. We then apply the same instance grouping.

    3.5 Extension to Dynamic Scenes

    For monocular video inputs, we extend LucidLyra to dynamic scenes by independently decoding a time-conditioned 3DGS state following Lyra’s bullet-time formulation [2, 53]. The same video model provides multi-view latents preserving input motion; the decoder predicts the full scene state at time τ, conditioned on source/target time encodings and query-time C-RADIO input-frame features F_τ:

    G̃_τ=D_3DGSᵈʸⁿ(Z,E,F_τ,Tˢʳᶜ,T_τᵗᵍᵗ).

    		(7)

    Initialized from the static model, the dynamic decoder trains with the same multi-task losses on τ-synchronized views. Dynamic scenes can only be supervised at the exact queried time, due to the changing scene. Following [Bahmani et al. [2]], we create six additional trajectories by processing the time-reversed input video and flipping it back. Each target frame is then paired with a same-time observation from a different viewpoint increasing multi-view supervision. Since each query time yields an independently decoded Gaussian state, we implement temporal instance tracking via an online prototype codebook inspired by IGGT4D [118]. At each query time, we represent each cluster by its normalized mean object embedding and greedily match cluster prototypes to codebook entries one-to-one above a cosine-similarity threshold. Matched clusters inherit persistent IDs and update the stored prototypes through averaging weighted by Gaussian count, while unmatched clusters initialize new IDs.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate LucidLyra’s joint generative 3D reconstruction and scene understanding on synthetic and real-image-conditioned scenes, followed by an analysis of its key components. Dynamic experiments, additional quantitative and qualitative results, downstream applications, and implementation details are provided in the appendix.

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Datasets. We augment Lyra-SDG [2] with semantic and instance teacher targets for training (Section3.3) and annotations for evaluation. Lyra-SDG uses GEN3C [72] to expand images and videos generated from diverse text prompts into multiple camera trajectories per scene. Its 59 031 static and 7 378 dynamic scenes contain RGB videos, camera poses, depth maps, and video latents. We preprocess teacher targets for all 53 million frames. A single image admits multiple plausible 3D completions. We evaluate agreement with fixed generated trajectories and their annotations. Our three curated 25-scene benchmarks use propagated reference annotations with human review and refinement: LucidLyra-SDG and LucidLyra-SDG Dynamic cover static and dynamic generated scenes, while LucidLyra-ADE20K uses real ADE20K validation images [114] to condition generated completions. All data and benchmarks will be released.

    For qualitative results, we generate input images with GPT Image or FLUX [62, 3]. For dynamic examples, we extend these to videos using Cosmos 3 [61]. We find that our method is agnostic to the choice of image-generation model.

    Evaluation. Following Lyra [2], we report PSNR and LPIPS [112] for reconstruction. Following [Li et al. [45], Xiong et al. [100], Li et al. [50], Li et al. [42]], we evaluate semantic segmentation using mIoU and mAcc over ADE20K classes present in each reference scene. Building on IGGT and video instance segmentation [42, 102], we evaluate cross-view instance consistency using the mean track precision–recall product (mTrackPR) and TrackPR25 at IoU 0.25 within ground-truth thing regions (SectionA.3).

    Baselines. We benchmark against existing 3D understanding methods combined with Lyra’s generative pipeline. Per-scene optimization: LangSplatV2, SFS, and Unified-Lift [45, 100, 116] fit feature fields on frozen Lyra Gaussians. Feed-forward: Chorus [50] processes frozen Lyra Gaussians, while IGGT [42] reconstructs geometry and instances directly from generated RGB videos. References: Reconstruction-only Lyra, alongside a teacher-lifting reference that directly assigns teacher features and instance IDs to frozen Lyra ray-aligned-Gaussians. The latter contextualizes the quality of our segmentation training signals.

    4.2 Evaluating Generative 3D Reconstruction and Understanding

    LucidLyra preserves reconstruction fidelity while adding understanding fields (Table1). Relative to Lyra, PSNR improves by 0.53/0.13 dB and LPIPS improves by 0.025/0.018 across benchmarks, confirming that our multi-task training does not degrade novel-view rendering quality.

    LucidLyra outperforms all two-stage baselines without per-scene optimization (Table1) in semantics, achieving 64.1/49.8 mIoU with synthetic and real-image conditioning, respectively. Plain LucidLyra exceeds the 3D-lifted teacher reference on SDG (64.1 vs. 60.5) and performs comparably on ADE20K (49.8 vs. 50.1). LucidLyra+ input-image 3D anchoring further boosts mIoU to 67.9/53.7.

    LucidLyra achieves 21.5/18.5 instance mTrackPR (Table1), outperforming the compared segmentation baselines in separating individual objects across generated viewpoints. Compared to the lifted teacher reference, mTrackPR is lower on SDG (21.5 vs. 22.8) and higher on ADE20K (18.5 vs. 17.3). LucidLyra+ gives a small SDG mTrackPR gain. Qualitative multi-view segmentations and feature PCAs are visualized in Fig.3.

    On a single NVIDIA A100 80 GB, teacher lifting, LangSplatV2, SFS, and Unified-Lift require 64, 697, 168, and 216 min to segment a single generated scene, respectively. This is dominated by foundation-model preprocessing. Feed-forward methods CHORUS and IGGT require 1.0 and 3.6 min, respectively, while LucidLyra and LucidLyra+ require 2.1 and 2.3 min. We measure wall-clock time from Lyra generated scenes (baselines) or video model latents (LucidLyra) to the final rgb, open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, and instance segmentation prediction.

    4.3 LucidLyra Analysis

    Losses and regularization. Removing C-RADIO [17] conditioning causes the largest drop in understanding: 7.2 mIoU and 6.6 mTrackPR points (Table2). Direct Gaussian semantic supervision adds 0.7 mIoU and 2.7 mTrackPR points beyond rendered supervision. Reconstruction masking and opacity pruning add 1.3 and 2.1 mTrackPR points, respectively, with small changes in reconstruction quality. Part-level supervision slightly improves mIoU and enables a more fine-grained scene interaction. The full model also retains reconstruction quality, slightly improving PSNR (25.02 vs. 24.88) and

    LPIPS (0.186 vs. 0.189) over the reconstruction-only control run. This control initializes from vanilla Lyra checkpoint and is trained identical to LucidLyra excluding our changes to the loss terms and architecture.

    Feature dimensions. Reducing the semantic feature dimension from 128 to 64 lowers mIoU by 1.4 points and mTrackPR by 1.0 point. A 256-dimensional representation exceeds the GPU memory budget. The chosen 128D achieves the best accuracy–memory trade-off among the tested settings. The 12-dimensional object-level instance representation achieves the highest mTrackPR among the tested settings: 21.5, compared with 19.3 at 8 dimensions and 18.1 at 16 dimensions. Semantic mIoU is unchanged at 8 dimensions and 1.0 point lower at 16 dimensions.

    Shared 3DGS decoder layers. Increasing the shared decoder depth from eight to twelve layers degrades reconstruction and understanding. Four shared layers remain competitive, while eight shared layers achieve the highest mTrackPR among the tested depths.

    4.4 Downstream Applications

    LucidLyra’s structured, queryable scenes directly enable downstream tasks including robotic simulation, 3D scene editing, and 3D asset mining (details and qualitative results in AppendixD).

    5 Conclusion

    We presented LucidLyra, which turns generated scenes into queryable 3D worlds by distilling generative and perceptual knowledge into a feed-forward Gaussian decoder. A camera-controlled video model supplies both latent representations and training data, enabling joint reconstruction and understanding without captured multi-view data, manual 3D annotations, or per-scene optimization. Experiments demonstrate improved semantic and instance understanding over the compared two-stage baselines while preserving Lyra’s reconstruction quality. Furthermore, we demonstrate initial results on dynamic scenes and applications in 3D scene editing, 3D asset mining, and physical-AI simulation. Future work could scale our approach by accelerated video generation [48] with larger-scale joint training for generation and scene understanding [13].
