To obtain high-quality reference annotations, we use an ensembled version of our SAM [34]/SAM2 [71] instance preprocessing, combined with human review, refinement, and assignment of ADE20K semantic labels. The resulting labels and persistent identities provide references across all six generated trajectories. Figure15 shows annotated examples.

    LucidLyra-ADE20K uses 25 diverse ADE20K validation images [114], selected for scene-category diversity. Gen3C [72] expands each image into six 121-frame videos. We use a SAM2 ensemble to propagate the original semantic and instance ground-truth labels through all camera trajectories, followed by human review and refinement. Figure16 shows example scenes.

    E.2 Dynamic Dataset

    Training data. The dynamic Lyra-SDG corpus comprises 7 378 video-conditioned scenes. Generation from the original and temporally reversed input video provides two complementary six-trajectory batches, each containing 121 synchronized frames per trajectory. Targets are constructed within each batch, keeping their independently initialized track IDs separate. Figure17 illustrates training scenes across viewpoints and time.

    Evaluation data. LucidLyra-SDG Dynamic contains 25 diverse curated scenes excluded from the training set. Annotation follows the static setup. Figure18 visualizes annotated examples.

    Appendix F Related Work

    Below, we discuss further related work not covered in the main paper.

    Dynamic representations

    Dynamic semantic and instance representations have likewise focused on captured video, spanning per-sequence optimization and feed-forward reconstruction. 4D LangSplat [46] fits language features to deformable 4D Gaussians, whereas TRASE [51] learns an instance field from per-frame masks. Related methods distill foundation-model features or temporal cues into scene-specific dynamic representations [37, 12, 115, 24, 20, 96, 27]. Feed-forward approaches amortize language-aligned dynamic reconstruction [97, 68], while IGGT4D [118] jointly predicts streaming geometry and persistent instances.

item.title: 换一套骨架就得重训？TopX 只吃骨架文件：73M 参数、flow matching，给未见过的骨骼直接生成动作 ｜ TopX: Text-to-Motion for Unseen Skeletons from the Skeleton File Alone
item.description:
一句话：不需要片段、模板、重定向或微调：输进运动学树、rest pose 与关节名就能出动作。

要点：

  • 现实约束：text-to-motion 模型一般只对训练时见过的骨架有效，而新角色到手往往只有一个骨架文件，没有动作片段、没有模板
  • TopX 是 73M 参数的 flow-matching Transformer，仅凭骨架的运动学树、rest pose 与关节名，就为任意骨架生成关节旋转与根轨迹
  • 归一化用 rest pose 与骨架尺度，rest pose 被编码成与「骨架怎么命名」无关的世界坐标描述子，从而支持跨骨架泛化

为什么值得看：角色资产管线里最贵的一步之一就是动作重定向。如果文本生成的动作能直接落在任意骨架上，等于把「新角色要有动作」这件事的门槛降到「有个骨架文件」。对做 NPC/动画批量生产的团队，这是可直接试的方向。

中文摘要：text-to-motion 模型通常只为训练时见过的骨架生成动作，而新的角色往往只以一个骨架文件的形式到手：没有该角色的动作片段、没有模板、也来不及做重定向或微调。TopX 研究这个「未见骨架」的设定，提出一个 7300 万参数的 flow-matching Transformer：仅凭骨架的运动学树、rest pose 与关节名称，就为任意骨架生成关节旋转与根轨迹。为支持跨骨架泛化，运动按 rest pose 与骨架尺寸归一化，rest pose 则被编码成一个与骨架命名方式无关的世界坐标描述子。它把「新角色要有动作」的门槛压到只剩一个骨架文件。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-28

本期推送：2026-11-02

TopX: Text-to-Motion for Unseen Skeletons from the Skeleton File Alone

Abstract

Text-to-motion models generate motion only for the skeletons they were trained on, while a new character arrives as a skeleton file and nothing else. We study text-to-motion for skeletons unseen in training, without clips of the character, templates, retargeting or fine-tuning. We present TopX, a 73M-parameter flow-matching transformer that generates joint rotations and a root trajectory for any skeleton from its kinematic tree, rest pose and joint names. Motion is normalised by the rest pose and the size of the skeleton, and the rest pose is encoded as a world-frame descriptor that is independent of how the rig’s author oriented each joint, while rest conventions are randomised during training. Attention is factorised over the joints and the frames of a motion. Across joints, queries and keys are rotated by HK-RoPE, a heat-kernel rotary encoding of the skeleton graph that is defined for every tree and does not change with the order of its joints or the eigenbasis of its Laplacian; across frames, they are rotated by a rotary encoding of frame order. To evaluate this generalisation, we build SkelShift, which unifies four motion corpora under one codec and holds out whole skeletons, tree classes and species, so that each test bucket isolates one kind of skeleton shift: topology, joint count, body plan, species or rig source. It scores motion quality without a learned evaluator. A single model animates every benchmark skeleton (4–117 joints) directly from its skeleton file and generates up to 240 frames. On held-out game species its motion is about as close to the real clips as two halves of the real clips are to each other (kernel distance 0.127 against 0.124), and text-to-motion retrieval reaches R@1 0.953, compared with 0.929 for real motion. Project page: https://chdtevior.github.io/TopX-page/.

1 Introduction

Text-to-motion generation has become highly capable for the human body [14, 41, 15, 11], and nearly all existing methods assume a single skeleton: the joint count, joint order and rest pose of the training body are built into the model. Games, film and virtual production animate large casts of non-human characters, each rigged with its own kinematic tree, joint names, joint order and rest pose. When such a character is created, only its skeleton file is available: there are no clips to normalise with, adapt to or retarget from. A text-to-motion model for such pipelines must therefore animate the skeleton from this file alone.

Three properties of a skeleton file make this challenging. Scale: without clips, the size of a character’s motion and the spread of each joint’s channels are unknown, so normalisation by per-rig motion statistics cannot be applied. Conventions: the order in which a file lists its joints, the names it gives them and the orientation of each joint’s rest frame are arbitrary choices of the rig’s author, on which the generated motion should not depend. Shape: the tree itself may lie outside the training distribution, with a new topology, more joints or an unfamiliar body plan. Existing approaches address these only in part: retargeting [43, 1] and template-based models [46, 45, 44] cannot represent skeletons beyond their template, and AnyTop [12] requires statistics of the target skeleton’s own motions.

The extent to which such models generalise remains unclear, because prior evaluations on unseen skeletons use only a handful of held-out skeleton types [31], held-out species sharing one topology [45], or no text conditioning [33]. Measuring generalisation requires held-out skeletons whose distance from the training data is controlled and reported, and metrics that remain valid on them; since the accuracy that a learned text–motion evaluator attains even on real motion can drop substantially outside its training distribution [45], we score motion quality with evaluator-free statistics.

To address these challenges, we make three contributions:

  • •

    TopX, a text-to-motion system for unseen skeletons. TopX is a 73M-parameter flow-matching transformer that animates any skeleton from its skeleton file alone (kinematic tree, rest pose and joint names), without clips of the target, retargeting or fine-tuning. Normalising motion by the rest pose handles scale without per-rig statistics, and the rest pose is described by a world-frame descriptor that is independent of the rig’s rest-frame conventions; the model outputs joint rotations and a root trajectory that drive the rig directly (Fig.1, Sec.3).

  • •

    HK-RoPE, a graph positional encoding for skeletons of arbitrary topology. To handle unseen tree shapes, HK-RoPE rotates attention queries and keys by heat-kernel coordinates of the skeleton graph, which are defined for every tree, invariant to joint relabelling and independent of the Laplacian eigenbasis (Sec.3.2).

  • •

    SkelShift, a dataset and benchmark for unseen skeletons. To make generalisation measurable, the dataset unifies four motion corpora under one codec: 143,334 captioned clips on skeletons of 4 to 142 joints, with every joint described in text. The benchmark holds out whole skeletons, tree classes and species in buckets along five axes of skeleton shift, reports each test tree’s distance to the training trees, and scores motion quality without a learned evaluator (Sec.4).

    • 2 Related Work

    Text-to-motion.

    Human text-to-motion has progressed from variational models [14] to diffusion in pose space [41, 50] or latent space [7] and to token-based models over quantised motion [48, 15], and has been extended with larger corpora [26, 11] and skeleton-aware latents [17]. Animal text-to-motion methods rely on a fixed template, such as the SMAL body model [46], a topology shared by humans and animals [45] or a unified 30-joint skeleton [44]; OmniSkel adapts a human model to new bone lengths [28]. All of these fix the kinematic tree, or at least its topology, at training time. In contrast, TopX fixes neither: a single model takes any kinematic tree as input, so a new character can be animated directly from its skeleton file.

    Motion on arbitrary skeletons.

    Retargeting maps motion between structurally compatible skeletons [43, 1] or through skeleton-agnostic embeddings [22, 51], and Motion2Motion [6] transfers across topologies from a few examples of the target. AnyTop [12] generates motion on arbitrary trees without text conditioning; it places the rest pose as the first frame, biases attention by tree distances, and normalises each skeleton by statistics of that skeleton’s own motions; UniMoGen [21] adds style and trajectory control on human skeletons. Text-conditioned generation across topologies has been demonstrated by OmniZoo [5], G-MDM [23], which predicts joint rotations without root translation, and ACT [30], which rigs a mesh and animates it from text. Concurrently with this work, UniMate [31] animates unseen skeletons zero-shot using a spectral rotary encoding of Laplacian eigenvectors, a graph attention bias, rest-pose rebasing and skeleton augmentation. TopX addresses the same setting but differs in four design choices: motion is normalised by the rest pose and the skeleton’s size, not by per-rig motion statistics; the rest pose is encoded by a world-frame descriptor that is independent of how each joint was oriented, and rest conventions are randomised during training; the joint coordinate of HK-RoPE is independent of the Laplacian eigenbasis, so the output does not change with joint order even under repeated eigenvalues; and one model generates up to 240 frames on skeletons of 4 to 117 joints.

    Evaluating unseen skeletons.

    UniMate holds out seven Truebones skeleton types (58 sequences) and reports a kinematic-feature FID and diversity, as well as foot sliding on 20 legged skeletons; X-MoGen [45] holds out species on its shared topology. For video-driven animation, TopoCap [33] separates seen and unseen topologies and MoCapAnything [13] stratifies seen, rare and unseen species; in retargeting, Hong et al. [18] report proportion changes and arbitrary structures separately. SkelShift brings such controlled axes of evaluation to text-conditioned generation. It tests whether a single model generalises to unseen topologies, rare body plans, joint counts outside the training range, new species and held-out Truebones rigs, and on each axis it measures how realistic the generated motion is, how well it keeps ground contact and, on held-out species, how well it matches the text. Held-out units are removed from training, the distance from every test tree to the training trees is reported, and results are broken down by axis.

    Positional encodings on graphs.

    Laplacian eigenvectors are ambiguous in sign and, within the eigenspace of a repeated eigenvalue, in the choice of basis [25, 19]. Diffusion-based coordinates avoid both: random-walk [10] and heat-kernel [40] signatures are well-established node encodings [34, 4], and WIRE [35] uses spectral and random-walk coordinates as rotary angles [39]. HK-RoPE adopts the heat-kernel signature as the rotary coordinate of a skeleton’s joints and pairs it with a rotary encoding of frame order.

    3 Method

    A rig ℝ=(T,Pʳᵉˢᵗ,ℕ) consists of a kinematic tree T over J joints, a rest pose (global joint positions Pʳᵉˢᵗ∈ℝ^J×3 and rest orientations Rʳᵉˢᵗⱼ), and joint names ℕ. Given ℝ and a caption c, TopX samples a motion x∈ℝ^L×J×17 from p_θ(x|ℝ,c) using a single transformer shared across all rigs. At generation time, no network input depends on a rig’s clips, so a rig unseen in training is handled exactly like a training rig. We apply this clip-free generation to every benchmark skeleton, whether seen or unseen in training.

    3.1 Representation and skeleton inputs

    Per-joint channels.

    A representation shared by all rigs must meet two requirements: it must be computable for any rigged animation from the kinematic tree, the rest pose and the motion alone, without a template skeleton, retargeting or inverse kinematics; and each channel must have the same meaning on every rig. We therefore describe every joint by the same 17 channels (Tab.5 in the appendix): (i) its position, with horizontal coordinates relative to the smoothed ground track of the root and absolute height, which decouples body pose from global displacement; (ii) its global rotation relative to its rest orientation, Rⱼ(f) R^rest⊤ⱼ at frame f, in the continuous 6D form [52], which equals the identity at the rest pose on every rig; (iii) its world velocity, used only as a supervision target; and (iv) a binary contact flag. The root additionally carries the ground track and the heading. Since velocities are never integrated, each frame can be decoded independently and without accumulated drift, either from the positions or by forward kinematics (FK) of the rotations, through two independent paths. The rotations and the root trajectory drive the rig, and all statistics in this paper are computed from them. The same conversion places the four corpora of SkelShift in a common representation (Sec.4.1).

    Rest normalisation.

    Rig sizes span several orders of magnitude, and a model without access to a rig’s clips cannot standardise its motion by their statistics. We centre every entry x_fjc (frame f, joint j, channel c) on the rig’s rest frame and scale it by the rig’s size:

    x̃_fjc=(x_fjc-xʳᵉˢᵗ_jc)/(σ_c),

    		(1)

    where xʳᵉˢᵗ is the rest pose written in the 17 channels (rest positions, identity rotations, zero velocity and contact, forward heading), and σ_c=s/g_c on the position, velocity and ground-track channels, where s is the diagonal of the rest pose’s bounding box and g_c is one of three global gains, and σ_c=1 on all other channels. At generation, the validity mask of an unseen rig follows from its structure alone: every joint carries the per-joint channels, and the root additionally carries the global ones.

    Per-joint features.

    Three features describe each joint and are added to all of its tokens (Sec.3.2). (i) A description, a short phrase such as “left thigh joint”, written from the joint’s name or, when the name is unrecognised or carries no anatomical meaning, from the tree’s geometry and, where annotated, the body plan; it is embedded once by a frozen LLM2Vec encoder [2]. Descriptions make joint semantics comparable across rigs: “front left upper leg” denotes the same concept on a horse and on a lizard, whereas raw names such as L_Femur_02 and b_hindleg_l_1 do not. (ii) A structural vector comprising the rest offset to the parent in the parent’s frame, the bone length, the depth, the path length to the root, the number of children and a leaf flag, mapped through a zero-initialised MLP. (iii) A world-frame rest descriptor: the world direction of the joint’s bone at rest and its rest position relative to the root’s ground point, expressed in units of the mean bone length and log-compressed. The parent-frame offset in (ii) depends on how the rig’s author oriented each joint’s rest frame; the world-frame descriptor does not, and it is the feature that conveys the rest pose to the network.

    3.2 Factorised attention with HK-RoPE

    A motion is a grid of tokens over two axes of different kinds: the joints of a frame form a tree that varies from rig to rig, whereas the frames of a joint form a sequence. TopX factorises attention along the two axes: each of its N_b blocks attends over time (one joint across its frames), then over joints (one frame across its joints), then applies an MLP. Position is encoded on both axes in the same way: queries and keys are RMS-normalised per head [8] and rotated by angles of their token’s position [39], so that position affects an attention logit only through the difference between the angles of the two tokens. The two encodings are designed jointly for skeleton graphs of arbitrary topology, and neither axis uses a learned table of absolute positions.

    Tokens and the rest frame.

    Each (frame, joint) pair forms one token: its 17 normalised channels are projected to width D. As in AnyTop [12], the rest pose is prepended to the sequence as a separate frame: the input [ xʳᵉˢᵗ|xᵗᵍᵗₜ ] consists of one clean rest frame, which is never noised, followed by L target frames that carry the flow interpolant and a learned marker; only the target frames are denoised. Under Eq.1, the rest frame is zero in every channel, so the target frames encode displacements from the rest pose of the given skeleton; the shape of the skeleton itself reaches the network through the per-joint features of Sec.3.1.

    Joint axis: HK-RoPE and tree bias.

    The joint axis requires a positional coordinate that (i) is defined for every tree, (ii) is invariant to the order in which the file lists the joints and to the eigenbasis returned by an eigensolver, and (iii) has the same dimension for any joint count, so that a single model applies to every skeleton. HK-RoPE (heat-kernel RoPE) derives this coordinate from the heat kernel of the skeleton graph. Let L=I-D^-1/2AD^-1/2 be the normalised Laplacian of the tree, with eigenpairs (λₖ,vₖ), 0=λ₀<λ₁≤…≤λ_J-1. For eight diffusion times τᵢ=2ⁱ⁻², i=0,…,7,

    hⱼ(τ)=∑ₖ₌₁^J-1e^-τλₖ vₖⱼ², h̃ⱼ(τ)=(hⱼ(τ))/(\tfrac1J∑ᵢhᵢ(τ)),

    		(2)

    and an MLP maps h̃ⱼ∈ℝ⁸ to the dₕ/2 angles θⱼ of joint j. The spatial attention of head h between joints i and j of a frame is then

    ℓ⁽ʰ⁾ᵢⱼ=(qᵢ^⊤R(θᵢ)^⊤R(θⱼ) kⱼ)/(√dₕ)+b⁽ʰ⁾ᵢⱼ=(qᵢ^⊤R(θⱼ-θᵢ) kⱼ)/(√dₕ)+b⁽ʰ⁾ᵢⱼ,

    		(3)

    where R(θ) rotates the dₕ/2 coordinate pairs of a query or key by the angles θ, so the joint coordinate enters only through θⱼ-θᵢ. The bias b⁽ʰ⁾ᵢⱼ, in the spirit of the graph-distance bias of AnyTop [12], is b⁽ʰ⁾ᵢⱼ=-\min(gᵢⱼ,8)+u⁽ʰ⁾_aᵢⱼ+d⁽ʰ⁾_sᵢⱼ; it depends on the hop distance gᵢⱼ and, through zero-initialised tables u and d, on the numbers of hops aᵢⱼ up and sᵢⱼ down to the lowest common ancestor, so that a head can distinguish a parent from its child and a limb from its counterpart on the other side of the body. hⱼ(τ) is the heat-kernel signature [40, 4] with the zero-eigenvalue mode removed, and it satisfies all three requirements. It is defined on every tree and has eight values per joint regardless of J: all J-1 non-trivial modes contribute, so no truncation or padding is needed. It does not depend on the eigenbasis: summed over an eigenspace, vₖⱼ² is the diagonal of the eigenspace’s projector, the same for every basis and every sign. Finally, relabelling the joints merely permutes its rows; since every other input is attached to a joint rather than to a slot, the motion predicted for each joint does not depend on the order in which the file lists the joints (proof in the appendix). In contrast, spectral rotary encodings of graphs derive their angles from Laplacian eigenvectors [35]; UniMate’s spectral joint encoding [31] resolves their sign ambiguity with a SignNet [25], but neither the basis ambiguity within a repeated eigenvalue nor the one introduced when truncation splits an eigenspace. This case is common: 3,210 of our 5,127 training skeletons (63%) have a repeated eigenvalue among the first eight non-trivial modes or between the eighth and the ninth.

    Frame axis.

    The temporal attention rotates queries and keys in the same way [39], by θ_f=f ω with ωₘ=700^-2m/dₕ, m=0,…,dₕ/2-1, for frame index f (the rest frame has f=0); the base of 700 is chosen for a 241-frame window.

    Text and time.

    The conditioning vector c=MLP(t)+MLP(e_c), where t is the flow time and e_c the pooled LLM2Vec embedding of the caption, produces the AdaLN shift, scale and gate of every sub-layer [32]; the text thus conditions the network through modulation only. The caption is dropped with probability 0.1 for classifier-free guidance [16]; the rest frame is never dropped.

    3.3 Training and sampling

    Objective.

    We train on the straight path xₜ=(1-t)ε+t x, ε∼ℕ(0,I), t∼U(0,1)[27, 29]; the network predicts the clean sample x̂ and is trained with a per-entry Huber loss, weighted by the velocity-space factor \max(1-t,σ_\min)⁻² of JiT [24] and normalised to unit mean over t. A 142-joint rig has 28 times as many body rows as a six-joint rig but the same single root row, so a plain mean over entries would let the body rotations of large rigs overwhelm the root trajectory and contacts of small ones. We partition the channels into nine groups g (position, rotation and velocity of the root and of the body; contact; ground track; heading) and use

    L=∑_gγ_g√N_g/N ℓ̄_g,

    		(4)

    where ℓ̄_g is the masked mean over the N_g valid entries of group g in the batch and N=∑_gN_g, so that a group’s share of the gradient does not grow with the number of entries it spans. The weights γ_g are computed from measured group energies so that each group receives a fixed target share of the objective (appendix). Auxiliary FK-consistency, world-velocity, foot-lock and acceleration terms are also added.

    Skeleton and convention augmentation.

    With probability 0.8, a training sample undergoes one kinematics-preserving operation: a joint is inserted on a bone, a few leaves are removed, single-child joints of a chain are merged, or every bone is rescaled by up to ±10%; the sample is then re-encoded by FK to remain self-consistent. Independently, with probability 0.5, every joint’s rest orientation is rotated randomly by up to 30^∘, as if the rig had been authored with another rest pose: the world motion is unchanged, and only the rest-relative rotations that the network must predict change. The changed rest pose reaches the network through the world-frame rest descriptor. Rigs are sampled with probability proportional to the square root of their clip count, so that corpora of single-clip rigs and of rigs with hundreds of clips both contribute.

    Sampling.

    Sampling integrates the straight path with S Euler steps, x←x+(x̂-x)/(S-i) at step i; invalid entries are kept at zero, and classifier-free guidance is applied to the caption only: x̂=x̂^∅+w (x̂ᶜ-x̂^∅). The output is used as generated, without grounding, foot locking or inverse kinematics.

    4 The SkelShift corpus and benchmark

    4.1 Four corpora under one codec

    SkelShift unifies four corpora under one codec (counts refer to training clips and rigs after the benchmark split is removed): the Objaverse-XL [9] subset of UniML3D [31] at a fixed commit (5,023 clips, 4,277 rigs, 6–60 joints), with one caption per clip written by a vision–language model; the AniMo4D animal library [44] (76,882 clips, 307 rigs) with its captions, together with HumanML3D [14] (26,844 clips on one 22-joint skeleton); further animations and species from the same game library as AniMo4D (29,645 clips, 485 rigs), captioned by rule from the animation names; and the Truebones zoo [42] (708 clips, 57 rigs, up to 142 joints). Training thus covers 139,102 clips (144 hours at 30 fps) on 5,127 rigs and 1,364 distinct trees, with 6 to 142 joints. All clips are encoded at 30 fps by the same codec, grounded at their lowest point, labelled with the same contact rule and passed through a data-quality check (appendix), so that every statistic has the same meaning across corpora. Since the source assets retain their original licences, the corpus will be released as per-clip source identifiers, splits and annotations, together with scripts that rebuild it from the originals and the metric code.

    4.2 Held-out buckets

    Each SkelShift bucket holds out a set of units (Tab.1). Two in-distribution buckets serve as references: ID-clip holds out clips of training rigs, and ID-tree holds out whole rigs whose tree is isomorphic to a training rig’s, so that only proportions, rest pose and names change. Each out-of-distribution bucket shifts along one axis. OOD-tree holds out a quarter of the rarely populated tree classes of bipeds and quadrupeds, and OOD-plan 40% of the tree classes of rare body plans (insects, birds, sea animals, snakes); every rig of a held-out class is removed from training. The OOD-J buckets contain the UniML3D rigs whose joint count lies outside that corpus’s training range: 61–117 joints (250 of which share Mixamo’s 65-joint humanoid tree) and 4 joints. OOD-species holds out four species of the game library—markhor and greater rhea (dev), capybara and emu (test)—with their male, female and juvenile rigs. OOD-new-species contains ten rigs of species absent from training (frogs, a newt, an axolotl, beetles, a cockroach, a leaf insect, a fruit bat, a terrapin), retained after a motion-quality check. OOD-rig contains eight Truebones quadrupeds (two bears, cat, goat, hound, lynx, stegosaurus, turtle) with unseen trees.

    Except in OOD-species, held-out units are assigned by hashing, one third to dev and two thirds to test; model selection and hyper-parameter choices for TopX use the dev split only. Every benchmark clip is annotated with the distance from its tree to the nearest training tree, its joint count and body plan, and whether its source motion was reused on a training skeleton, so that results can be stratified by any of these annotations.

    4.3 Protocol and metrics

    Generation.

    TopX animates every benchmark rig, including those of ID-clip, from its skeleton file: the tree, the rest pose, the joint names and the up and forward axes. For each clip, five samples are generated with different seeds at the length of the real clip (capped at 240 frames), using the guidance scale with the lowest KIDdesc on dev (appendix), and scored without post-processing.

    Motion quality.

    We measure Fréchet distances on kinematic features, computed on the animation that drives the rig, i.e. the FK of the generated rotations together with the root trajectory:

  • •

    FIDkin: Fréchet distance between the generated and the real clips of a group, computed on the public kinetic features of Bailando [38] and Motion2Motion [6], which UniMate’s FID also uses [31]: per joint, the mean horizontal and vertical kinetic energy and the mean acceleration over the clip, with positions in units of the rig scale. Pooling them over joints by mean and standard deviation yields six features for every skeleton; both sets are standardised by the real clips, and each group must contain at least 50 real clips.

  • •

    FIDdesc: the same distance on the 24 kinematic descriptors of our scorer (below), which also cover pose, contact, rhythm and path.

    • Per bucket, our scorer (appendix) reports KIDdesc, a kernel distance [3] on the same 24 kinematic descriptors per clip (speeds, accelerations, contact, turning, pose spread, path), standardised by the training clips, which remains well defined on small groups and is reported together with its real–real value, i.e. the KID between two halves of the real clips; Slip, the share of grounded joint-frames that slide, computed over all joints using the codec’s contact rule; Pen., the share of frames whose lowest joint is more than 0.005 s below the ground; Float, the share of clips (excluding those with airborne captions) that hover higher than 95% of the training clips of their body plan; and Speed, the joint speed relative to the real clips. All statistics are averaged over seeds and weight rigs equally, except KIDdesc, which compares clip distributions.

    Text alignment.

    We measure text alignment by text-to-motion retrieval with a skeleton-agnostic evaluator trained on our training split (appendix), within the rigs of the held-out game species (439 test clips with curated captions, pools of 8, chance level 0.125). TopX reaches R@1 0.953, compared with 0.929 for the real motions and 0.120 with shuffled captions. Figure2 shows qualitative examples.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：不需要片段、模板、重定向或微调：输进运动学树、rest pose 与关节名就能出动作。

要点：

  • 现实约束：text-to-motion 模型一般只对训练时见过的骨架有效，而新角色到手往往只有一个骨架文件，没有动作片段、没有模板
  • TopX 是 73M 参数的 flow-matching Transformer，仅凭骨架的运动学树、rest pose 与关节名，就为任意骨架生成关节旋转与根轨迹
  • 归一化用 rest pose 与骨架尺度，rest pose 被编码成与「骨架怎么命名」无关的世界坐标描述子，从而支持跨骨架泛化

为什么值得看：角色资产管线里最贵的一步之一就是动作重定向。如果文本生成的动作能直接落在任意骨架上，等于把「新角色要有动作」这件事的门槛降到「有个骨架文件」。对做 NPC/动画批量生产的团队，这是可直接试的方向。

中文摘要：text-to-motion 模型通常只为训练时见过的骨架生成动作，而新的角色往往只以一个骨架文件的形式到手：没有该角色的动作片段、没有模板、也来不及做重定向或微调。TopX 研究这个「未见骨架」的设定，提出一个 7300 万参数的 flow-matching Transformer：仅凭骨架的运动学树、rest pose 与关节名称，就为任意骨架生成关节旋转与根轨迹。为支持跨骨架泛化，运动按 rest pose 与骨架尺寸归一化，rest pose 则被编码成一个与骨架命名方式无关的世界坐标描述子。它把「新角色要有动作」的门槛压到只剩一个骨架文件。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-28

本期推送：2026-11-02

TopX: Text-to-Motion for Unseen Skeletons from the Skeleton File Alone

Abstract

Text-to-motion models generate motion only for the skeletons they were trained on, while a new character arrives as a skeleton file and nothing else. We study text-to-motion for skeletons unseen in training, without clips of the character, templates, retargeting or fine-tuning. We present TopX, a 73M-parameter flow-matching transformer that generates joint rotations and a root trajectory for any skeleton from its kinematic tree, rest pose and joint names. Motion is normalised by the rest pose and the size of the skeleton, and the rest pose is encoded as a world-frame descriptor that is independent of how the rig’s author oriented each joint, while rest conventions are randomised during training. Attention is factorised over the joints and the frames of a motion. Across joints, queries and keys are rotated by HK-RoPE, a heat-kernel rotary encoding of the skeleton graph that is defined for every tree and does not change with the order of its joints or the eigenbasis of its Laplacian; across frames, they are rotated by a rotary encoding of frame order. To evaluate this generalisation, we build SkelShift, which unifies four motion corpora under one codec and holds out whole skeletons, tree classes and species, so that each test bucket isolates one kind of skeleton shift: topology, joint count, body plan, species or rig source. It scores motion quality without a learned evaluator. A single model animates every benchmark skeleton (4–117 joints) directly from its skeleton file and generates up to 240 frames. On held-out game species its motion is about as close to the real clips as two halves of the real clips are to each other (kernel distance 0.127 against 0.124), and text-to-motion retrieval reaches R@1 0.953, compared with 0.929 for real motion. Project page: https://chdtevior.github.io/TopX-page/.

1 Introduction

Text-to-motion generation has become highly capable for the human body [14, 41, 15, 11], and nearly all existing methods assume a single skeleton: the joint count, joint order and rest pose of the training body are built into the model. Games, film and virtual production animate large casts of non-human characters, each rigged with its own kinematic tree, joint names, joint order and rest pose. When such a character is created, only its skeleton file is available: there are no clips to normalise with, adapt to or retarget from. A text-to-motion model for such pipelines must therefore animate the skeleton from this file alone.

Three properties of a skeleton file make this challenging. Scale: without clips, the size of a character’s motion and the spread of each joint’s channels are unknown, so normalisation by per-rig motion statistics cannot be applied. Conventions: the order in which a file lists its joints, the names it gives them and the orientation of each joint’s rest frame are arbitrary choices of the rig’s author, on which the generated motion should not depend. Shape: the tree itself may lie outside the training distribution, with a new topology, more joints or an unfamiliar body plan. Existing approaches address these only in part: retargeting [43, 1] and template-based models [46, 45, 44] cannot represent skeletons beyond their template, and AnyTop [12] requires statistics of the target skeleton’s own motions.

The extent to which such models generalise remains unclear, because prior evaluations on unseen skeletons use only a handful of held-out skeleton types [31], held-out species sharing one topology [45], or no text conditioning [33]. Measuring generalisation requires held-out skeletons whose distance from the training data is controlled and reported, and metrics that remain valid on them; since the accuracy that a learned text–motion evaluator attains even on real motion can drop substantially outside its training distribution [45], we score motion quality with evaluator-free statistics.

To address these challenges, we make three contributions:

  • •

    TopX, a text-to-motion system for unseen skeletons. TopX is a 73M-parameter flow-matching transformer that animates any skeleton from its skeleton file alone (kinematic tree, rest pose and joint names), without clips of the target, retargeting or fine-tuning. Normalising motion by the rest pose handles scale without per-rig statistics, and the rest pose is described by a world-frame descriptor that is independent of the rig’s rest-frame conventions; the model outputs joint rotations and a root trajectory that drive the rig directly (Fig.1, Sec.3).

  • •

    HK-RoPE, a graph positional encoding for skeletons of arbitrary topology. To handle unseen tree shapes, HK-RoPE rotates attention queries and keys by heat-kernel coordinates of the skeleton graph, which are defined for every tree, invariant to joint relabelling and independent of the Laplacian eigenbasis (Sec.3.2).

  • •

    SkelShift, a dataset and benchmark for unseen skeletons. To make generalisation measurable, the dataset unifies four motion corpora under one codec: 143,334 captioned clips on skeletons of 4 to 142 joints, with every joint described in text. The benchmark holds out whole skeletons, tree classes and species in buckets along five axes of skeleton shift, reports each test tree’s distance to the training trees, and scores motion quality without a learned evaluator (Sec.4).

    • 2 Related Work

    Text-to-motion.

    Human text-to-motion has progressed from variational models [14] to diffusion in pose space [41, 50] or latent space [7] and to token-based models over quantised motion [48, 15], and has been extended with larger corpora [26, 11] and skeleton-aware latents [17]. Animal text-to-motion methods rely on a fixed template, such as the SMAL body model [46], a topology shared by humans and animals [45] or a unified 30-joint skeleton [44]; OmniSkel adapts a human model to new bone lengths [28]. All of these fix the kinematic tree, or at least its topology, at training time. In contrast, TopX fixes neither: a single model takes any kinematic tree as input, so a new character can be animated directly from its skeleton file.

    Motion on arbitrary skeletons.

    Retargeting maps motion between structurally compatible skeletons [43, 1] or through skeleton-agnostic embeddings [22, 51], and Motion2Motion [6] transfers across topologies from a few examples of the target. AnyTop [12] generates motion on arbitrary trees without text conditioning; it places the rest pose as the first frame, biases attention by tree distances, and normalises each skeleton by statistics of that skeleton’s own motions; UniMoGen [21] adds style and trajectory control on human skeletons. Text-conditioned generation across topologies has been demonstrated by OmniZoo [5], G-MDM [23], which predicts joint rotations without root translation, and ACT [30], which rigs a mesh and animates it from text. Concurrently with this work, UniMate [31] animates unseen skeletons zero-shot using a spectral rotary encoding of Laplacian eigenvectors, a graph attention bias, rest-pose rebasing and skeleton augmentation. TopX addresses the same setting but differs in four design choices: motion is normalised by the rest pose and the skeleton’s size, not by per-rig motion statistics; the rest pose is encoded by a world-frame descriptor that is independent of how each joint was oriented, and rest conventions are randomised during training; the joint coordinate of HK-RoPE is independent of the Laplacian eigenbasis, so the output does not change with joint order even under repeated eigenvalues; and one model generates up to 240 frames on skeletons of 4 to 117 joints.

    Evaluating unseen skeletons.

    UniMate holds out seven Truebones skeleton types (58 sequences) and reports a kinematic-feature FID and diversity, as well as foot sliding on 20 legged skeletons; X-MoGen [45] holds out species on its shared topology. For video-driven animation, TopoCap [33] separates seen and unseen topologies and MoCapAnything [13] stratifies seen, rare and unseen species; in retargeting, Hong et al. [18] report proportion changes and arbitrary structures separately. SkelShift brings such controlled axes of evaluation to text-conditioned generation. It tests whether a single model generalises to unseen topologies, rare body plans, joint counts outside the training range, new species and held-out Truebones rigs, and on each axis it measures how realistic the generated motion is, how well it keeps ground contact and, on held-out species, how well it matches the text. Held-out units are removed from training, the distance from every test tree to the training trees is reported, and results are broken down by axis.

    Positional encodings on graphs.

    Laplacian eigenvectors are ambiguous in sign and, within the eigenspace of a repeated eigenvalue, in the choice of basis [25, 19]. Diffusion-based coordinates avoid both: random-walk [10] and heat-kernel [40] signatures are well-established node encodings [34, 4], and WIRE [35] uses spectral and random-walk coordinates as rotary angles [39]. HK-RoPE adopts the heat-kernel signature as the rotary coordinate of a skeleton’s joints and pairs it with a rotary encoding of frame order.

    3 Method

    A rig ℝ=(T,Pʳᵉˢᵗ,ℕ) consists of a kinematic tree T over J joints, a rest pose (global joint positions Pʳᵉˢᵗ∈ℝ^J×3 and rest orientations Rʳᵉˢᵗⱼ), and joint names ℕ. Given ℝ and a caption c, TopX samples a motion x∈ℝ^L×J×17 from p_θ(x|ℝ,c) using a single transformer shared across all rigs. At generation time, no network input depends on a rig’s clips, so a rig unseen in training is handled exactly like a training rig. We apply this clip-free generation to every benchmark skeleton, whether seen or unseen in training.

    3.1 Representation and skeleton inputs

    Per-joint channels.

    A representation shared by all rigs must meet two requirements: it must be computable for any rigged animation from the kinematic tree, the rest pose and the motion alone, without a template skeleton, retargeting or inverse kinematics; and each channel must have the same meaning on every rig. We therefore describe every joint by the same 17 channels (Tab.5 in the appendix): (i) its position, with horizontal coordinates relative to the smoothed ground track of the root and absolute height, which decouples body pose from global displacement; (ii) its global rotation relative to its rest orientation, Rⱼ(f) R^rest⊤ⱼ at frame f, in the continuous 6D form [52], which equals the identity at the rest pose on every rig; (iii) its world velocity, used only as a supervision target; and (iv) a binary contact flag. The root additionally carries the ground track and the heading. Since velocities are never integrated, each frame can be decoded independently and without accumulated drift, either from the positions or by forward kinematics (FK) of the rotations, through two independent paths. The rotations and the root trajectory drive the rig, and all statistics in this paper are computed from them. The same conversion places the four corpora of SkelShift in a common representation (Sec.4.1).

    Rest normalisation.

    Rig sizes span several orders of magnitude, and a model without access to a rig’s clips cannot standardise its motion by their statistics. We centre every entry x_fjc (frame f, joint j, channel c) on the rig’s rest frame and scale it by the rig’s size:

    x̃_fjc=(x_fjc-xʳᵉˢᵗ_jc)/(σ_c),

    		(1)

    where xʳᵉˢᵗ is the rest pose written in the 17 channels (rest positions, identity rotations, zero velocity and contact, forward heading), and σ_c=s/g_c on the position, velocity and ground-track channels, where s is the diagonal of the rest pose’s bounding box and g_c is one of three global gains, and σ_c=1 on all other channels. At generation, the validity mask of an unseen rig follows from its structure alone: every joint carries the per-joint channels, and the root additionally carries the global ones.

    Per-joint features.

    Three features describe each joint and are added to all of its tokens (Sec.3.2). (i) A description, a short phrase such as “left thigh joint”, written from the joint’s name or, when the name is unrecognised or carries no anatomical meaning, from the tree’s geometry and, where annotated, the body plan; it is embedded once by a frozen LLM2Vec encoder [2]. Descriptions make joint semantics comparable across rigs: “front left upper leg” denotes the same concept on a horse and on a lizard, whereas raw names such as L_Femur_02 and b_hindleg_l_1 do not. (ii) A structural vector comprising the rest offset to the parent in the parent’s frame, the bone length, the depth, the path length to the root, the number of children and a leaf flag, mapped through a zero-initialised MLP. (iii) A world-frame rest descriptor: the world direction of the joint’s bone at rest and its rest position relative to the root’s ground point, expressed in units of the mean bone length and log-compressed. The parent-frame offset in (ii) depends on how the rig’s author oriented each joint’s rest frame; the world-frame descriptor does not, and it is the feature that conveys the rest pose to the network.

    3.2 Factorised attention with HK-RoPE

    A motion is a grid of tokens over two axes of different kinds: the joints of a frame form a tree that varies from rig to rig, whereas the frames of a joint form a sequence. TopX factorises attention along the two axes: each of its N_b blocks attends over time (one joint across its frames), then over joints (one frame across its joints), then applies an MLP. Position is encoded on both axes in the same way: queries and keys are RMS-normalised per head [8] and rotated by angles of their token’s position [39], so that position affects an attention logit only through the difference between the angles of the two tokens. The two encodings are designed jointly for skeleton graphs of arbitrary topology, and neither axis uses a learned table of absolute positions.

    Tokens and the rest frame.

    Each (frame, joint) pair forms one token: its 17 normalised channels are projected to width D. As in AnyTop [12], the rest pose is prepended to the sequence as a separate frame: the input [ xʳᵉˢᵗ|xᵗᵍᵗₜ ] consists of one clean rest frame, which is never noised, followed by L target frames that carry the flow interpolant and a learned marker; only the target frames are denoised. Under Eq.1, the rest frame is zero in every channel, so the target frames encode displacements from the rest pose of the given skeleton; the shape of the skeleton itself reaches the network through the per-joint features of Sec.3.1.

    Joint axis: HK-RoPE and tree bias.

    The joint axis requires a positional coordinate that (i) is defined for every tree, (ii) is invariant to the order in which the file lists the joints and to the eigenbasis returned by an eigensolver, and (iii) has the same dimension for any joint count, so that a single model applies to every skeleton. HK-RoPE (heat-kernel RoPE) derives this coordinate from the heat kernel of the skeleton graph. Let L=I-D^-1/2AD^-1/2 be the normalised Laplacian of the tree, with eigenpairs (λₖ,vₖ), 0=λ₀<λ₁≤…≤λ_J-1. For eight diffusion times τᵢ=2ⁱ⁻², i=0,…,7,

    hⱼ(τ)=∑ₖ₌₁^J-1e^-τλₖ vₖⱼ², h̃ⱼ(τ)=(hⱼ(τ))/(\tfrac1J∑ᵢhᵢ(τ)),

    		(2)

    and an MLP maps h̃ⱼ∈ℝ⁸ to the dₕ/2 angles θⱼ of joint j. The spatial attention of head h between joints i and j of a frame is then

    ℓ⁽ʰ⁾ᵢⱼ=(qᵢ^⊤R(θᵢ)^⊤R(θⱼ) kⱼ)/(√dₕ)+b⁽ʰ⁾ᵢⱼ=(qᵢ^⊤R(θⱼ-θᵢ) kⱼ)/(√dₕ)+b⁽ʰ⁾ᵢⱼ,

    		(3)

    where R(θ) rotates the dₕ/2 coordinate pairs of a query or key by the angles θ, so the joint coordinate enters only through θⱼ-θᵢ. The bias b⁽ʰ⁾ᵢⱼ, in the spirit of the graph-distance bias of AnyTop [12], is b⁽ʰ⁾ᵢⱼ=-\min(gᵢⱼ,8)+u⁽ʰ⁾_aᵢⱼ+d⁽ʰ⁾_sᵢⱼ; it depends on the hop distance gᵢⱼ and, through zero-initialised tables u and d, on the numbers of hops aᵢⱼ up and sᵢⱼ down to the lowest common ancestor, so that a head can distinguish a parent from its child and a limb from its counterpart on the other side of the body. hⱼ(τ) is the heat-kernel signature [40, 4] with the zero-eigenvalue mode removed, and it satisfies all three requirements. It is defined on every tree and has eight values per joint regardless of J: all J-1 non-trivial modes contribute, so no truncation or padding is needed. It does not depend on the eigenbasis: summed over an eigenspace, vₖⱼ² is the diagonal of the eigenspace’s projector, the same for every basis and every sign. Finally, relabelling the joints merely permutes its rows; since every other input is attached to a joint rather than to a slot, the motion predicted for each joint does not depend on the order in which the file lists the joints (proof in the appendix). In contrast, spectral rotary encodings of graphs derive their angles from Laplacian eigenvectors [35]; UniMate’s spectral joint encoding [31] resolves their sign ambiguity with a SignNet [25], but neither the basis ambiguity within a repeated eigenvalue nor the one introduced when truncation splits an eigenspace. This case is common: 3,210 of our 5,127 training skeletons (63%) have a repeated eigenvalue among the first eight non-trivial modes or between the eighth and the ninth.

    Frame axis.

    The temporal attention rotates queries and keys in the same way [39], by θ_f=f ω with ωₘ=700^-2m/dₕ, m=0,…,dₕ/2-1, for frame index f (the rest frame has f=0); the base of 700 is chosen for a 241-frame window.

    Text and time.

    The conditioning vector c=MLP(t)+MLP(e_c), where t is the flow time and e_c the pooled LLM2Vec embedding of the caption, produces the AdaLN shift, scale and gate of every sub-layer [32]; the text thus conditions the network through modulation only. The caption is dropped with probability 0.1 for classifier-free guidance [16]; the rest frame is never dropped.

    3.3 Training and sampling

    Objective.

    We train on the straight path xₜ=(1-t)ε+t x, ε∼ℕ(0,I), t∼U(0,1)[27, 29]; the network predicts the clean sample x̂ and is trained with a per-entry Huber loss, weighted by the velocity-space factor \max(1-t,σ_\min)⁻² of JiT [24] and normalised to unit mean over t. A 142-joint rig has 28 times as many body rows as a six-joint rig but the same single root row, so a plain mean over entries would let the body rotations of large rigs overwhelm the root trajectory and contacts of small ones. We partition the channels into nine groups g (position, rotation and velocity of the root and of the body; contact; ground track; heading) and use

    L=∑_gγ_g√N_g/N ℓ̄_g,

    		(4)

    where ℓ̄_g is the masked mean over the N_g valid entries of group g in the batch and N=∑_gN_g, so that a group’s share of the gradient does not grow with the number of entries it spans. The weights γ_g are computed from measured group energies so that each group receives a fixed target share of the objective (appendix). Auxiliary FK-consistency, world-velocity, foot-lock and acceleration terms are also added.

    Skeleton and convention augmentation.

    With probability 0.8, a training sample undergoes one kinematics-preserving operation: a joint is inserted on a bone, a few leaves are removed, single-child joints of a chain are merged, or every bone is rescaled by up to ±10%; the sample is then re-encoded by FK to remain self-consistent. Independently, with probability 0.5, every joint’s rest orientation is rotated randomly by up to 30^∘, as if the rig had been authored with another rest pose: the world motion is unchanged, and only the rest-relative rotations that the network must predict change. The changed rest pose reaches the network through the world-frame rest descriptor. Rigs are sampled with probability proportional to the square root of their clip count, so that corpora of single-clip rigs and of rigs with hundreds of clips both contribute.

    Sampling.

    Sampling integrates the straight path with S Euler steps, x←x+(x̂-x)/(S-i) at step i; invalid entries are kept at zero, and classifier-free guidance is applied to the caption only: x̂=x̂^∅+w (x̂ᶜ-x̂^∅). The output is used as generated, without grounding, foot locking or inverse kinematics.

    4 The SkelShift corpus and benchmark

    4.1 Four corpora under one codec

    SkelShift unifies four corpora under one codec (counts refer to training clips and rigs after the benchmark split is removed): the Objaverse-XL [9] subset of UniML3D [31] at a fixed commit (5,023 clips, 4,277 rigs, 6–60 joints), with one caption per clip written by a vision–language model; the AniMo4D animal library [44] (76,882 clips, 307 rigs) with its captions, together with HumanML3D [14] (26,844 clips on one 22-joint skeleton); further animations and species from the same game library as AniMo4D (29,645 clips, 485 rigs), captioned by rule from the animation names; and the Truebones zoo [42] (708 clips, 57 rigs, up to 142 joints). Training thus covers 139,102 clips (144 hours at 30 fps) on 5,127 rigs and 1,364 distinct trees, with 6 to 142 joints. All clips are encoded at 30 fps by the same codec, grounded at their lowest point, labelled with the same contact rule and passed through a data-quality check (appendix), so that every statistic has the same meaning across corpora. Since the source assets retain their original licences, the corpus will be released as per-clip source identifiers, splits and annotations, together with scripts that rebuild it from the originals and the metric code.

    4.2 Held-out buckets

    Each SkelShift bucket holds out a set of units (Tab.1). Two in-distribution buckets serve as references: ID-clip holds out clips of training rigs, and ID-tree holds out whole rigs whose tree is isomorphic to a training rig’s, so that only proportions, rest pose and names change. Each out-of-distribution bucket shifts along one axis. OOD-tree holds out a quarter of the rarely populated tree classes of bipeds and quadrupeds, and OOD-plan 40% of the tree classes of rare body plans (insects, birds, sea animals, snakes); every rig of a held-out class is removed from training. The OOD-J buckets contain the UniML3D rigs whose joint count lies outside that corpus’s training range: 61–117 joints (250 of which share Mixamo’s 65-joint humanoid tree) and 4 joints. OOD-species holds out four species of the game library—markhor and greater rhea (dev), capybara and emu (test)—with their male, female and juvenile rigs. OOD-new-species contains ten rigs of species absent from training (frogs, a newt, an axolotl, beetles, a cockroach, a leaf insect, a fruit bat, a terrapin), retained after a motion-quality check. OOD-rig contains eight Truebones quadrupeds (two bears, cat, goat, hound, lynx, stegosaurus, turtle) with unseen trees.

    Except in OOD-species, held-out units are assigned by hashing, one third to dev and two thirds to test; model selection and hyper-parameter choices for TopX use the dev split only. Every benchmark clip is annotated with the distance from its tree to the nearest training tree, its joint count and body plan, and whether its source motion was reused on a training skeleton, so that results can be stratified by any of these annotations.

    4.3 Protocol and metrics

    Generation.

    TopX animates every benchmark rig, including those of ID-clip, from its skeleton file: the tree, the rest pose, the joint names and the up and forward axes. For each clip, five samples are generated with different seeds at the length of the real clip (capped at 240 frames), using the guidance scale with the lowest KIDdesc on dev (appendix), and scored without post-processing.

    Motion quality.

    We measure Fréchet distances on kinematic features, computed on the animation that drives the rig, i.e. the FK of the generated rotations together with the root trajectory:

  • •

    FIDkin: Fréchet distance between the generated and the real clips of a group, computed on the public kinetic features of Bailando [38] and Motion2Motion [6], which UniMate’s FID also uses [31]: per joint, the mean horizontal and vertical kinetic energy and the mean acceleration over the clip, with positions in units of the rig scale. Pooling them over joints by mean and standard deviation yields six features for every skeleton; both sets are standardised by the real clips, and each group must contain at least 50 real clips.

  • •

    FIDdesc: the same distance on the 24 kinematic descriptors of our scorer (below), which also cover pose, contact, rhythm and path.

    • Per bucket, our scorer (appendix) reports KIDdesc, a kernel distance [3] on the same 24 kinematic descriptors per clip (speeds, accelerations, contact, turning, pose spread, path), standardised by the training clips, which remains well defined on small groups and is reported together with its real–real value, i.e. the KID between two halves of the real clips; Slip, the share of grounded joint-frames that slide, computed over all joints using the codec’s contact rule; Pen., the share of frames whose lowest joint is more than 0.005 s below the ground; Float, the share of clips (excluding those with airborne captions) that hover higher than 95% of the training clips of their body plan; and Speed, the joint speed relative to the real clips. All statistics are averaged over seeds and weight rigs equally, except KIDdesc, which compares clip distributions.

    Text alignment.

    We measure text alignment by text-to-motion retrieval with a skeleton-agnostic evaluator trained on our training split (appendix), within the rigs of the held-out game species (439 test clips with curated captions, pools of 8, chance level 0.125). TopX reaches R@1 0.953, compared with 0.929 for the real motions and 0.120 with shuffled captions. Figure2 shows qualitative examples.

item.title: 把家具从房间里「擦掉」还不能把墙擦歪：LoRA 微调让提示词编辑器学会守几何 ｜ Finetuning Prompt-Based Image Editor for Geometry-Consistent Room Defurnishing
item.description:
一句话：FLUX.2 这类编辑器真实感够、结构忠实度不够；用布局条件 + LoRA 微调把两头拿回来。

要点：

  • 任务：从单张房间图里抹掉全部家具，得到空房间——用于 diminished reality 与虚拟布景等 XR 应用
  • 两头都难：既要把家具区域补得像真的，又不能把房间的 3D 几何弄歪；提示词驱动的编辑器（如 FLUX.2）真实感强，但结构忠实度不如显式布局条件的 inpainting
  • 做法是给这类编辑器设计一套 LoRA 微调配方，把几何一致性补回来，从而同时拿到「真实感」与「结构忠实」

为什么值得看：实景转场景（XR、虚拟布景、数字孪生）最怕「补完墙是歪的」。这条说明了一个可复用的工程套路：不要换模型，而是用数据把现成编辑器的几何先验调回来。

中文摘要：从单张房间图像里抹掉全部家具、得到空房间，对 diminished reality、虚拟布景等 XR 应用很有价值。这个任务有两重难点：既要把家具区域补得真实，又不能扭曲房间的 3D 几何。提示词驱动的图像编辑器（如 FLUX.2）在真实感上表现突出，但结构忠实度不如显式布局条件引导的 inpainting。作者因此提出一套针对这类编辑器的 LoRA 微调配方，用训练把几何一致性补回来，从而同时获得「补得真」与「结构不歪」两个性质。对把实拍转成可用场景资产的管线，这条给的是一条成本较低的改进路径：不换模型，用数据把现成编辑器的几何先验调回来。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-25

本期推送：2026-11-02

Finetuning Prompt-Based Image Editor for Geometry-Consistent Room Defurnishing

Abstract

Erasing all furniture from a single room image to generate its empty counterpart is valuable for XR applications such as diminished reality and virtual staging. The challenge is twofold: inpainting the furniture regions with realistic content, and doing so without distorting the room’s 3D geometry. Prompt-driven image editors, such as FLUX.2, handle realism impressively, but their structural faithfulness is inferior to explicit layout conditioned inpainting. To improve geometric consistency, we propose a training recipe for finetuning a LoRA on 2,500 furnished-empty room pairs. FLUX.2 with our LoRA adaptor significantly improves geometric consistency while retaining the high texture fidelity. This single-photo inpainter can be an effective building block for depth-aware and 3D-consistent XR pipelines.

Defurnishing is the virtual removal of furniture from a photo, 3D scan, or other digital representation of a room for XR applications such as diminished reality and virtual staging (fig:vstaging). Achieving it requires not only inpainting furniture and their shadows, but also preserving geometric consistency so that reconstructed walls and floors remain faithful to the underlying room structure [4]. Such consistency is particularly important in AR and MR, where virtual objects are anchored to the physical environment. Diminished reality (DR) is an established XR problem that aims to remove or conceal real-world objects while maintaining a coherent scene appearance [6]. Recent DR methods leverage explicit scene geometry through structure-aware RGB-D inpainting [2] or by restoring background scene content from pre-captured 3D Gaussian Splat representations [8]. In contrast, we focus on improving prompt-based editing from a single RGB image. Our lightweight LoRA adaptation can serve as the generative inpainting module within future depth-aware and 3D XR pipelines.

We focus on removing all furniture from a single RGB image to generate an empty-room image. One way to preserve structure is through layout-guided per-plane inpainting [4], but it is not robust to shadows and often introduces artifacts in non-planar regions. Prompt-based image editors such as FLUX.2 [1] and Qwen-Image-Edit [9] produce highly realistic edits but offer no explicit geometric constraints. This raises our central question: How geometrically consistent are prompt-based editors for defurnishing, and how can we improve them?

We compare layout-guided Stable Diffusion (SD) inpainting against FLUX.2 using LPIPS [11] to measure texture fidelity and Layout Error [3] to measure geometric consistency. To improve FLUX.2’s geometric consistency, we propose a lightweight LoRA finetuning recipe on 2,500 furnished-empty room pairs. FLUX.2 with our LoRA adaptor achieves the best texture fidelity and geometric consistency across all three methods, as shown qualitatively in fig:teaser.

1 Method

We compare three inpainting approaches (fig:approaches), given as input an RGB image and a binary mask of the furniture regions. The mask can be either user defined or derived using segmentation models. For LoRA finetuning, we collect and prepare a dataset of 2,500 furnished-empty room pairs in-house.

1.1 SD + LoRA + ControlNet

We condition Stable Diffusion 1.5 (SD1.5) inpainting with the room layout. Since the base SD1.5-inpainting often leaves residual furniture shadows, we also finetune a LoRA on our dataset of furnished-empty pairs. Layout is estimated via a 3D layout extractor [5], which uses perceptual cues such as depth and semantic segmentation to localize the wall and floor planes in 3D. We render depth and normal maps from this model and feed them to SD1.5-inpainting through two ControlNets [10], each at a condition weight of α=0.5.

1.2 FLUX.2

We apply the mask to the RGB image, marking the masked regions with magenta. We then use the 4-step distilled version of FLUX.2[klein] [1] on the masked image with the prompt:

This is a photo of a room in which all objects are marked with a magenta mask. Remove all the masked regions and their shadows from this photo, while ensuring that all the unmarked regions remain absolutely unchanged.

With no geometric conditioning, this serves as a reference point for evaluating the structural consistency of a purely prompt-driven editor.

1.3 FLUX.2 + LoRA

To improve geometric consistency, we adapt FLUX.2[klein] by finetuning a LoRA (rank 64, alpha 32) on an in-house dataset of 2,500 furnished-empty room pairs. Inputs are a masked RGB image and a prompt, same as the previous approach. We train for 3,000 steps, with learning rate 1×10⁻⁴, batch size 4, height 768, ema-decay 0.999. Differential guidance is turned on to encourage focus on inpainted areas. Training is done using ai-toolkit[7] on a single NVIDIA A5000, and takes 12 hours. During inference, the LoRA is applied onto the distilled 4-step model.

1.4 Evaluation metrics

We evaluate the defurnishing pipelines along two criteria: texture fidelity and geometric consistency. For texture fidelity we report the standard perceptual similarity score, LPIPS, on a test-set of 300 furnished-empty room pairs. For geometric consistency we report Layout Error on a test-set of 100 furnished room images annotated with layout boundaries. Layout Error is the distance of each annotated layout boundary pixel to the nearest predicted one [3]. The predicted layout is the boundary of the ‘floor’ region, extracted from semantic segmentation of the inpainted image.

Layout Error=(1/|G|)∑_g∈G\min(d(g,P), τ),

(1)

where G and P are the ground-truth and predicted edge pixels, d(g,P)=\min_p∈P∥g-p∥ the distance to the nearest predicted edge, and τ a threshold capping the penalty for severely missed boundaries.

2 Results and Conclusion

tab:quantitative summarizes the performance of the three methods. SD+LoRA+ControlNet achieves lower Layout Error than FLUX.2 due to explicit layout conditioning, but obtains worse LPIPS scores, reflecting the stronger image synthesis capability of FLUX.2. Although FLUX.2 produces realistic edits, it can distort room geometry since it is a generalist model, not optimized for preserving geometry. Our lightweight LoRA adaptation specializes FLUX.2 for defurnishing by learning task-specific geometric cues, including vanishing lines, room element sizes, and scene layout. Consequently, FLUX.2 with our LoRA adaptor achieves the best performance on both texture fidelity and geometric consistency.

To conclude, generalist prompt-based image editors achieve high visual realism but lack geometric faithfulness for room defurnishing, which our lightweight LoRA adaptation recovers while retaining texture fidelity. Our approach is image-only: it uses no explicit 3D conditioning and builds no persistent scene representation, so multi-view and temporal consistency are not guaranteed. Inference takes up to 5 seconds per image, so our method currently supports offline scene preparation rather than real-time XR. Future work will incorporate explicit geometry through depth or normal conditioning, and the resulting model can distill faster real-time variants or precompute empty-room assets for DR systems such as DimSplat [8].

Acknowledgements.

AI assistance was used for figure formatting and proofreading.

（参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 人群模拟的泛化该被真正测一遍：Trajeform 把轨迹数据嵌成表示，再检验它对真实场景的迁移 ｜ Trajeform: Embedding Crowd Data
item.description:
一句话：人群模拟器的能力高度依赖训练数据的类型与多样性，而现有泛化指标几乎测不出这点。

要点：

  • 目标：让 crowd simulation 生成的 agent 行为更丰富、自然，并贴合所处环境；近年用机器学习直接从轨迹数据学出行为模式，能捕捉越来越复杂的人群动力学
  • 但作者指出，这些系统的能力**强烈依赖训练数据的类型与多样性**——换个场地、换个密度分布就可能失效
  • 文章主张把「数据」本身嵌成表示（Trajeform），并指出多数现有指标在评估「模拟器泛化到真实数据集」时存在明显缺陷，需要更合适的衡量方式

为什么值得看：人群/交通这类模拟在引擎里常被当作「参数调一调就行」，实际瓶颈是训练数据覆盖不到的场景。把数据表示与泛化度量一起摆上台面，比再加一个损失项更有价值——尤其对做开放世界人流、活动疏散的团队。

中文摘要：人群模拟的目标是生成丰富、自然且与环境相称的 agent 行为。近年来机器学习让这类行为可以直接从轨迹数据中学到，模型因此能捕捉越来越复杂的人群动力学；但作者指出，这些系统的能力强烈依赖训练时所用数据的类型与多样性，一旦面对分布不同的真实数据集就未必成立。文章提出 Trajeform，把人群数据本身嵌入成一种表示，并讨论如何更合理地评估「模拟器对真实世界数据集的泛化」——因为现有的大多数指标在这一维度上存在明显局限。对把人群模拟当作管线一环的引擎团队，这篇提醒的是：先看数据覆盖，再谈模型能力。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-30

本期推送：2026-11-02

Trajeform: Embedding Crowd Data

Abstract

Crowd simulation aims to generate agent behaviours that are rich, natural, and appropriate to their surrounding environment. Recent advances in Machine Learning have enabled such behavioural patterns to be learned directly from trajectory data, allowing simulation models to capture increasingly complex crowd dynamics. However, the capabilities of these systems remain strongly dependent on the type and diversity of the data used during training. When evaluating how well crowd simulators generalise to real-world datasets, most existing metrics focus primarily on trajectory-level differences rather than behaviour-level similarity. In this paper, we present Trajeform, a framework that trains a reconstruction VAE (Variational Autoencoder) on real trajectory data to learn a meaningful continuous embedding that preserves behavioural characteristics of real crowds. The trained encoder can then be applied to synthetic trajectories generated by simulators and used to compare the resulting embedding distributions. Additionally, the learned embedding can be used to analyse supplementary data, such as trajectories corresponding to a simulator’s principal behaviours or captured data from controlled environments (e.g., cycling), providing insight into their ability to span the real behavioural embedding space. The framework compares data from three simulators (CCP, modCCP, and RVO) against ground-truth datasets and is evaluated quantitatively and qualitatively using latent-space analysis, distributional metrics, and trajectory generation through sampling from the aggregated posterior distribution. The results indicate that the learned latent space captures meaningful trajectory dependencies found in the real data, making the framework useful both as an additional measure of synthetic data believability and as a tool for informing the training of future trajectory models.

I Introduction

Crowd simulation aims to populate virtual environments with realistic agent movements. Within this scope, the umbrella of realism includes behaviour diversity, richness, and contextual awareness, in that agents should not only move naturally, but also behave in ways that are appropriate to the environment, e.g., a university campus. Extensive research has achieved advanced simulators for generating believable agents [1, 2, 3], utilised in crowd authoring to optimise simulator parameter spaces with respect to an authoring constraint [4, 5]. However, most of these systems either rely on manual parameterisation [1], or synthetic data [4]. Works that utilise real data are often constrained by the amount and type of data they use (single policy [6], controlled environments [7, 8]), hence hindering generalisability. Therefore, it is imperative to measure behavioural similarity by comparing differently sourced agent behaviours with real data [9]. In this work, we aim to quantify and formalise an embedding representation to assess the quality of agent behaviours in comparison with real ones. Such a tool enables comparing real and simulated behaviours in the representation space, and informing a selection of parameters spanning the real data features.

Measuring behaviour similarity properly, in the context of crowds, is a challenging undertaking due to the conceptual definition of a behaviour “match” and its non-deterministic nature. Relevant works weigh hand-crafted salient features [10, 5], perceptually validate realism [11, 12], or combine both (perceptually-validated metric) [13]. However, these works still focus on trajectory faithfulness, and are biased either on the selection of trajectory features, or the expertise of user study participants. Other works utilise entropy-based measures [14, 15]. To compare simulated and real data, several systems [16, 4] report metrics on trajectory features such as Deviation From Goal (DFG), and Optimal Path (OP) [17]. Even though these metrics are widely used and can give strong indications regarding the distribution of trajectory features in the two groups (generated and real), they are more tailored to trajectory features in an aggregated manner (e.g., DFG for all agents at every timestep); these partially capture behavioural aspects (turning left and turning right contain the same behaviour but lead to different paths) or limit controllability. We aim to investigate learnable features to complement the assembly of metrics used for comparing between two sets of behaviours.

In this paper, we introduce Trajeform, a trajectory-based framework that learns an embedding space directly from real crowd trajectory data. The learned latent distribution serves as a baseline, against which synthetic trajectories (e.g., generated by crowd simulators) can be compared. Synthetic trajectories are projected onto the learned latent space, allowing their inferred distributions to be juxtaposed with the real-data embedding distribution. The framework preserves the properties of a VAE latent space while encouraging behaviourally similar trajectories to cluster together. Since the model is trained through trajectory reconstruction, the decoder can additionally be used to project latent embeddings back into the trajectory space. Trajeform primarily aims to project crowd data onto an embedding space tailored to real behavioural features. To achieve this, the framework operates on canonicalised trajectories aligned during preprocessing, encouraging the model to focus on behavioural characteristics beyond simple positional attributes such as spawn location or orientation. Consequently, the learned embedding space captures more behaviour-relevant representations. Beyond measuring behaviour similarity, the framework can also provide indications regarding how effectively a simulator spans the real-data behavioural manifold, while additionally informing simulator parameter selections towards distributions more consistent with the arrangement of real data in the latent space. We evaluate the proposed framework through comparisons with established quantitative metrics, complemented by graphical analyses of the learned embedding distributions.

In a nutshell, we deliver a model trained on real data, that transforms trajectories to learned latent features. The trained latents compile a distribution used as a baseline for comparisons with differently-sourced data, e.g., simulated. Hence, our contribution can be summarised as follows:

  • •

    Learning to embed crowd data in a feature space aligned with real behavioural characteristics, and

  • •

    Inferring a latent distribution from real data embeddings, enabling informed sampling, and similarity measurement in latent space.

    • II Related Work

    II-ATrajectory-based Metrics

    To compare simulations—either with synthetic or real data—various quantitative metrics have been proposed. At the macroscopic level, the Fundamental Diagram [18] is widely used, relating speed, density, and flow to capture global crowd phenomena. At the microscopic level, metrics focus on per-trajectory features such as deviation from goals, path optimality, and distance to nearest neighbours, which can indicate behaviours like grouping. Another approach compares distributions of trajectory features, such as speed and position. Several crowd simulators leverage fundamental diagrams and low-level features for validation [16, 1, 6]. However, such metrics are more tailored to trajectory replication instead of behaviour similarity and so they are often sensitive to outliers or detailed motions [19, 20]. Some works benchmark evaluations, but specifically for steering behaviours [21]. Charalambous et al. [22] propose a method for outlier detection through a data-driven approach, while Lerner et al. [23] perform database matching. More recently, Wang et al. [9] employ Bayesian inference to discover latent path patterns from trajectory data for the analysis and comparison of crowd behaviours. Our method is complementary to other techniques, and does not perform inference on the trajectory space, but on a compressed latent representation using an end-to-end architecture.

    Perhaps closer to our method is Crowd Space [15] that defines agent descriptors (Minimal Predicted Distance) and trains a dimensionality reduction model to find the most suitable simulator for a given real scenario. This method learns a manifold based on the proposed agent-centric entropy [15, 14]. In our method however, we do not specify the evaluation metric, but instead, allow the model to learn features freely, and derive a metric post-training, using our learned manifold. Also, we employ a variational model, improving the sampling and generative capabilities. Crowd Space aims to assess the predictive accuracy of simulators to find the best simulation method to use on new crowd scenarios. Our method focuses on learning meaningful embeddings from real data, emphasising representation rather than classification. Crowd Space in trained on a larger set of real data that includes controlled and dense environments [7, 24], whereas we aim at in-the-wild behaviours. Finally, in Trajeform, we do not group our trajectories according to their scenario source, e.g., University Campus, but rather, learn a collective representation since behaviours in two different scenarios could be the same.

    II-BPerceptual Evaluation

    Apart from using quantitative methods to evaluate trajectory and behaviour plausibility, perceptual evaluation is also explored as a way to mitigate for the aforementioned metric limitations. User studies have been implemented to assess trajectory realism [25, 26, 27, 28]. O’Connor et al. [29] conduct a study to determine whether users find crowd behaviours to be more realistic with a Social Force model, and its implications in psychophysical experimentation. Smaller user studies have also been conducted as part of a larger evaluation protocol of proposed optimisation models [4], or authoring tools [30] asking users to report on believability and usability. Still, user studies, especially in the domain of virtual crowds, are highly dependent on the study design, the experience of participants in the domain, and general visualisation aspect of the shown stimuli, e.g., body animation, clothing, facial animation, and environment quality [31, 32]. Daniel et al. [13] propose a quality metric that combines comparison metrics with perceptual tools. Although existing quantitative and qualitative evaluation approaches have been proven useful in uncovering certain behavioural aspects of simulated agents, in our method we compare directly with real data, using learned features and so alleviating the need to hand-craft quantitative metrics but also avoid the perceptual biases. Our method can be used as an additional approach, complementary to other metrics.

    II-CTrajectory Representation

    Representing trajectories and trajectory-based behaviours is also important for analysis and comparisons. Morphable Crowds by Ju et al. [7] employs a data-driven method to build a trajectory model and create behaviour prefabs, while GREIL by Charalambous et al. [6] learns an inverse Reinforcement Learning policy from real data. Pure trajectory information usually has higher dimensionality p=(t,x,z)∈(T,2) and contains low-interpretability features in terms of behavioural characteristics, e.g., assigning behaviour labels to a distribution of positional data is not straightforward. Therefore, multiple works have attempted to transform pure trajectories to some compressed representations, e.g., trajectory images [4, 33], trajectory parameters [5]. Additional works employ learning-based methods to encode trajectory information into high-level parameters, e.g., combination of common behaviours [1], and OCEAN personality attributes [34]. High-level trajectory embeddings enhance explainability and assist comparison and analysis, however, the extracted features are dependent on the data used, which is often not sourced from real scenarios. Conversely, approaches based on real data, lack controllability and generalisability [35], especially if said data come from controlled settings instead of in-the-wild. Here, we strive for an embedding based on real, in-the-wild data, employing a learning-based method to allow the model freedom to learn appropriate behavioural and trajectory features that would be challenging to define through traditional feature specification.

    II-DCrowd Data

    Having crowd data is essential for improving simulation systems, as it supports data-driven methods [23] and provides training data for ML models. While both synthetic and real data can be used, real datasets are preferable because they capture complex, hard-to-replicate crowd dynamics. Such data can be used for training (if sufficiently large) or for evaluating new simulators [36, 15]. Crowd data typically consists of agent trajectories, including at least 2D positions and often orientations. Ideally, datasets would be paired, containing ground truth annotations (e.g., behavioural descriptions), which are crucial for supervised learning. However, collecting such data is challenging. Trajectories are usually obtained either through video tracking or motion capture, with data gathered in controlled settings [7, 8] or in real environments ranging from sparse to dense crowds [24, 37]. Due to the difficulty of large-scale motion capture, most datasets rely on video-based tracking. Widely used datasets include those from [38, 39], covering environments such as a church yard, a shopping street, and a university campus, as well as video-based datasets like [40]. Despite these efforts, there remains a lack of large paired datasets, limiting the ability of learning-based approaches to extract behaviour patterns. As a result, many works rely on synthetic data tailored to their specific needs.

    III Overview

    III-AProblem Definition

    First, let us define some notations. Let T⊆ℝ²ˣᵀ be the trajectory space, where T is the maximum trajectory length, associated with path duration which is measured in number of frames - directly corresponding to duration (s) since timestep is kept fixed. Also in the trajectory space, let τᵗ be the 2D position at time t, with τ∈T a trajectory point. We define τ_C to be the set of category-specific trajectories, with C={R,S,G} denoting real, synthetic, and generated, respectively.

    Our goal is to train an encoder E_θ:T→ℤ, subject to parameters θ, that creates a mapping from the trajectory space to the latent space ℤ⊆ℝ^Z with latent dimensions Z, where latent point z∈ℤ. Given the trained encoder, real data τ_R and simulated trajectories τ_f,h, we can obtain z_R,z_f and zₕ via zᵢ=E_θ(τᵢ). If there are simulators f:ℙ_f→T and h:ℙₕ→T, where ℙᵢ a simulator-specific parameter space, suppose that f,h attempt to simulate the real data. Then, comparing the distributions of z_f and zₕ against z_R, we can provide an indication of how well they represent the real data distribution. If τ_f,h are two different datasets to be used for training a trajectory model, the latent distribution comparisons help indicate how close the training set would be to the existing real data - a measure analogous to class balancing.
